name: Burundi Colline Masenga
short_description: The profile is on the delicate and bright side for Burundi, with elegant acidity that weaves through complex raw sugar sweetness. Top notes hint at cinnamon stick, rose hips tea, and lemon. Excellent pour-over. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: We've really enjoyed the light/bright aspects found in this year's coffee from Masenga. Compared to the others in the box, the profile is a bit more delicate and high-toned, with elegant acidity that weaves through complex sweetness at lighter roast levels. The fragrance had a maple sugar note that was quite potent, with sprinkles of unrefined sugar, and complex baking spices. The wet aromatics were a bit more spice-forward, all spice and cinnamon notes layered with dark sugar,  honey, and a hint of orange. Some of that spiced complexity comes through in the cup too, well-integrated and balanced, and sits nicely with the assemblage of raw sugar notes that inform the core cup sweetness. As the coffee cools, the delicate aspects start to outline more distinct flavors of cinnamon stick, chamomile and rose hips teas, along with a hint of lemon essence. These aspects bring quite a bit of interest to light City roasts, and lighter body paired with tartaric acidity shines a light on Masenga's crisp cup profile.
farm_notes: This coffee comes from the Masenga hill ("colline") region, and part of a cluster of hilltop villages that we bought coffee from this year. It's opposite of Migoti hill, which you may be familiar with from our site. In fact, this coffee is from the same group, headed by a man named Dan Brose, and his partner Poncien. They buy coffee from the surrounding hillsides and then process it at their wet milling site in Migoti. With plenty of washing tanks, Migoti is well-equipped to manage lot separations in order to isolate different qualities during the main part of the harvest. They have two sets of tanks and the coffee is fermented in 2 stages. The first stage is dry fermentation, where the coffee is poured into the cement tanks without water. After 12 hours, fermentation is well underway. The coffee is then moved to a second tank where water is added and the process continues for another half-day, after which it is soaked in clean water for 4 to 6 hours. Once the fruit mucilage is completely washed away, the coffee is moved to what are called "skin drying tables" where it is hand sorted for defects that are easiest to see while the coffee is still wet. Finally, the coffee is moved to raised beds and dried the rest of the way down to 11% moisture. Check out our podcast episode with Dan Brose , where we learn more about his background in coffee and growing up in Burundi.

name: Burundi Monge Murambi Hill
short_description: Syrupy bodied coffee with clean, bright flavors that are sweet from start to finish. Cane sugar and honey sweetness, hints of English Breakfast tea, orange essence, mouth-cleansing acidity. The complete package! City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: There's honey sweetness in the fragrance, with hints of vanilla cream soda, and aromatic maple sugar. The wet grounds also had a potent array of raw sugar notes that imbued the steam, along with accents of chocolate-covered fruit, loose leaf herbal tea, and dried berry. The hot cup starts off much simpler than the smells might lead on. But give it some time and the profile opens up as it cools. The profile is bright and clean, sweet from start to finish, and syrupy-bodied. City and City+ roasts show elements of raw cane sugar and honey, opening up to hints of English Breakfast tea, and orange essence. The acidity has a brisk quality that's also very tea-like, with pleasant bittering notes of tannic tea, and shaved citrus rind. I found the light roasts to the complete package; so sweet, nuanced and bright. The perfect coffee for pour-over brewing if there ever was one! Full City roasts were quite nice as well. The bittersweetness is more robust, interspersed with a note of star anise that brings some aromatic complexity to the low tones.
farm_notes: Not to be confused with "Murambi" in Kiganda, another coffee we've bought in the past (and again this year too!), this lot is from Mutambu Commune near the Monge Nature Reserve in Bujumbura. The coffee washing station is at a lower elevation than the coffee, which grows in the surriounding the steep hillside reaching over 2000 meters above sea level. Murambi is the name of one of the hilltop villages, or "collines", and the farmers from Mutambu sell their coffee to the station below. They are one of 4 hilltop villages that the folks who run the wet mill buy from, the others being Rugembe, Masenga and Migoti. This is the first year we've bought coffee from this group, going all in with lots from each colline. The coffee is depulped using a 3-disc depulper, fermented with water and graded in long cement washing channels. Before drying on long, raised drying beds, the wet parchment drip-dries on small screens where any physical defects that can be identified by sight are removed. Check out our podcast episode with Dan Brose , where we learn more about his background in coffee and growing up in Burundi.

name: Burundi Mutambu Migoti Hill
short_description: Excellent light roast brew, elegant, bright, with prevalent sweetness, and top note highlights of cherry, raw sugar, spice tea, rose hips, and a twist of lemon. Dark roasts are best for espresso. City to Full City. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Layered sweetness is a pervading characteristic in both light and dark roasts, however we felt that dark roasts were best for espresso, rather than brewed coffee. Light roasts have a sparkle of acidity that shines through the sweetness, perfect for a pour-over brew or iced coffee. Maple sweet smells come on strong in the ground coffee, with hints of light brown sugar, and a hint of sweetened chocolate. The wet aroma is also very sweet and refined, with notes of light brown sugar and malt syrup, accented by hints of cherry and loose leaf tea. The cup is bright and refreshing, with notes of cranberry and a twist of lemon that cuts through base raw sugar sweetness. The coffee expresses elegance as it cools, with delicate body, and top note highlights of rose hips, demerara sugar, spice tea, and zested citrus are revealed as it cools. At Full City, semi-sweet chocolate flavors cool to a slightly fruit/cocoa construct, like dark cocoa powder and raisin. I preferred Full City as espresso, where notes caramelized sugars and dark cacao are distilled down into the syrupy-texture, along with a subtle aromatic hint of anise, and a grabby orange note that pulls at the sides of your tongue.
farm_notes: This coffee is from a station called "Migoti", also the name of the hill on which it's built. The Migoti mill was built in the last 10 years, and is made up of relatively new equipment, which in and of itself has advantages. The management has done an excellent job of organizing the workflow from wet mill to drying beds too. With plenty of washing tanks, Migoti is well-equipped to manage lot separations in order to isolate different qualities during the main part of the harvest. They have two sets of tanks and the coffee is fermented in 2 stages. The first stage is dry fermentation, where the coffee is poured into the cement tanks without water. After 12 hours, fermentation is well underway. The coffee is then moved to a second tank where water is added and the process continues for another half-day, after which it is soaked in clean water for 4 to 6 hours. Once the fruit mucilage is completely washed away, the coffee is moved to what are called "skin drying tables" where it is hand sorted for defects that are easiest to see while the coffee is still wet. Finally, the coffee is moved to raised beds and dried the rest of the way down to 11% moisture. The coffee in this lot is from the surrounding Migoti farmers, but they are also buying from 3 other hills: Rugembe, Murambi (not to be confused with Murambi station, which we also buy) and Masenga.

name: Colombia Huila EA Decaf
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Typica Types, Modern Hybrids
appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 15-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination
short_description: Sweetly balanced with hints of fruit that lend to a lively acidic impression for decaf coffee. Notes of barley malt, honey, fresh green apple, cinnamon, cocoa powder. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: The bright, fruit accents this decaf produced on the cupping table were a nice surprise! The dry grounds had a clean cane sugar sweetness, fruit accents of apple and dried peach, and milk chocolate. Pouring the hot water brought out a bit of cinnamon spice bread, mixed with dried fruit hints. This brews such a well-rounded cup at City/City+ roast level, and quite fruited for decaf. The profile is highlighted by raw sugar sweetness, and hints of fruit that bring out a pleasantly moderate level of acidity. Base sweetness hinted at barley malt and honey, striking a nice balance of sweet and lower-toned cocoa flavors as it cooled. Fruit notes come into play as well, a hint at green apple has a tangy aspect, spice accent of pear baked with cinnamon, and an acidic impression that points to pineapple juice. It should definitely take to darker roast levels too, though we haven't roasted many batches beyond Full City at this point (I'll report back when we do). EA decafs tend to have good body for carrying roast tones well, and this lot is no exception.
farm_notes: This decaf blend comes from several small farms in Colombia's Southern Department of Huila. Colombia's coffee growing communities are largely made up of what are considered "small producers", with close to 95% managing 5 hectares or less. These are typically wet processed coffees, using small pulping machinery at home, fermented to remove the outer mucilage layer, then dried inside small drying rooms that help protect the coffee from the elements. The coffee is decaffeinated right in Colombia. The plant is called Descafecol, located in Manizales, Caldas. It's a state-of-the-art facility, partly owned by Coffein Compagnie from Germany. The method used is direct contact type using Ethyl Acetate, which can be naturally derived from fruits and vegetables, thus is generally referred to as a natural decaf method (often called "sugar cane decaf").

name: Colombia Huila La Argentina
short_description: Versatile Colombia, from mid-toned semi-sweet chocolate and tarry burnt sugars, to intense cocoa roast flavors and thick body when roasted dark. Great coffee for milk drinks. City+ to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: City+ roast level is a good place to start, but La Argentina holds up to 2nd Crack too. At City+, the grinds had a honey wheat bread scent, with notes of barley malt and bittersweet cocoa. The wet aroma offered some semi-sweet chocolate notes, along with herbal-accented sugars. The cup is pleasantly mild, with mid-toned flavors of semi-sweet chocolate and tarry burnt sugars that connect to bittering cocoa in the aftertaste. As it cools, a subtle suggestion of dried fruit brings out a soft acidic dimension, and hints of buckwheat and green herb mark the finish. Full City+ roasts are intensely low-toned and on the bittering end of the spectrum, roasted cacao nibs, baking chocolate and hints of dark-roasted grains. It's a profile perfect for milk drinks and made for espresso.
farm_notes: This lot is a blend from small producers in La Argentina town, within Colombia's southern Huila department. The coffee is grown between 1600 and 1900 meters, and most of the farms are planted in a mix of Caturra, Variedad Colombia, Castillo. The last lot we bought from this group had a fruit-forward cup profile, due in part to the long fermentation times they implement. It's very common for farmers to ferment their coffee for 3-4 days, which can have a pretty profound impact on the cup. This lot is much more straightforward, built on bittersweet, mid-toned flavors. It's made an excellent dark roast brew, and will work great as espresso too.

name: Colombia Productores de Buesaco
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids, Typica Types
short_description: This small producer blend from Buesaco has made such a well-rounded brewed coffee, toffee and creamy caramel sweetness accented by notes of baked apple, pear butter, milk chocolate, and juicy acidity. City to Full City+.
full_cupping_notes: This small producer Buesaco blend has made such a well-rounded brewed coffee, creamy dark sweetness from start to finish, with fruit accents as it cools, and moderate, mouth refreshing acidity. The fragrance has toffee sweetness accented by fruited hints, potent dark caramelized notes, with a note of green grape. Caramelized sweetness carries through to the wet aroma, punchy and out front, like torched sugar desserts, while breaking through the crust releases notes of baked fruits in the steam. The cup has very nice underlying sweetness, creamy caramel and toffee, with milk chocolate and bittersweet accents. As it cools, fruit flavors start to emerge, like baked apple and pear butter start, as well as mouth refreshing acidity has fruit juice appeal. The aftertaste trails off to some darker cocoa notes that leave a lasting impression on the palate, and bodes well for roasting this coffee to darker levels (we haven't tested ourselves yet!).
farm_notes: This is a small producer blend made up from coffee farms near Buesaco town, in Colombia's Nariño Department. We put this blend together after cupping several samples from the region, the goal being to separate out any coffees that hit our quality target. The local coffee association is a newer venture started by two brothers who stepped out on their own to offer a more direct and transparent option than some of the local competitors. Association membership continues to grow, and we're always presented with some truly impressive coffees, including on our Summer 2025 visit to their warehouse cupping lab. Farms are typically planted in Caturra and Variedad Colombia (F4 and F6 types), grown at altitudes between 1700 and 2000 meters, and each contributing lot in this batch are fully washed.

name: Costa Rica Red Honey El Coyote Typica
short_description: Punchy bittersweets fade to berry-toned impressions as it cools, with notes of spiced dark chocolate, burnt caramel, blackberry, dried cherry, chocolate raspberry truffle, palm sugar and rustic cocoa. City to Full City+.
full_cupping_notes: Between brewing this coffee and cupping it from a spoon, I had very different impressions. In both cases, I found flavors of fruit and chocolate, with plump body that comes off a bit juicy. But the brewed coffee came off much more balanced in terms of fruits, and the roast bittering was more intense too. I didn't roast it dark, but the flavors indicate that this will make a steller dark roasted honey process for those who appreciate hefty roast-tones and chocolate. The fragrance and aroma had a dried berry note wrapped in bittersweet cocoa and rustic sugars, with hints of rice syrup and chocolate granola. The brewed coffee has punchy cocoa up front that fades to berry-toned impressions as the coffee cools, hinting at blackberry, dried cherry, and cinnamon-spiced dark chocolate.They sit well together, and the cup cools to unrefined palm and date sugars, with rustic dark cocoa and burnt caramel in the aftertaste. For a somewhat fruited coffee, the acidity is fairly mild, even when roasted light.
farm_notes: The "El Coyote" farm is run by Horacio and Alejandro Solis, in Tarrazu's Talamanca Sierra highland region, where they operate the Don Oscar micro mill, a name honoring their late father, Oscar Solis, who originally planted coffee on this land. Their farm is broken into 40 different lots, each with distinct demarcation, and a different mix of varieties. El Coyote is planted in Typica, Villalobos and Catuaí, and stretches upward of 2000 meters above sea level. This red honey process lot is a separation of Typica from the farm, which they have the least of and only amounted to 5 bags. "Honey" process method involves pulping the outer cherry while leaving the sticky fruit mucilage intact to the coffee seeds during the drying phase. It turns a reddish color when dry, which is how it got the name "red honey". We often find that red honey coffees have fruitier flavors than washed, and while I wouldn't call this coffee "fruity", it certainly offers fruit accents, along with body and rich bittersweetness. Honey process coffees tend to present darker when roasting, and also produce a lot of chaff. It's not hard to roast, per se, but you should pay closer attention to time and the audible snaps, rather than physical coloring for judging roast degree. This small, 5 bag lot is only available in 1# bags.

name: Costa Rica Tarrazu Beneficio Los Angeles
short_description: The cup intensity comes off a bit like honey process coffee, moderately fruited, round body and rustic-sweetness underneath. Notes of dark corn syrup, dried peach, fig bar, apricot tea, raw nut and carob. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: This lot from Los Angeles shows a unique fruited cocoa flavor, accented by rustic-tinged sweetness and a fairly mild acidic impression. It came off more like a honey process coffee to us and a bit more intense than a classic washed coffee. It smelled of caramelized sugars when ground, milk chocolate, and dried stone fruits. The wet aroma pulls out more of the plum fruit notes, poached pear and peach, with intense raw sugars and a mild cocoa overlay. The brewed coffee shows some moderate fruit accents, dried peach, fig bar, and date, with a grainy element to the sweetness that brings to mind dark corn syrup. As it cools, the brew gives off some molasses tones to the sweetness, along with apricot tea, and a bittering aspect that brings to mind apple skins. It's an interesting cup, and I think some will find a milder acidic impression to be a plus. Full City roasts have a unique chocolate flavor, a bit like carob, with raw nut undertones, and fruit syrup as it cools. It's been fun to try different brew methods, and I'm currently enjoying the body that I'm getting from a Clever Dripper.
farm_notes: Beneficio Los Angeles is located in the famed Dota region of Tarrazú, and is owned and operated by Lizeth Castillo, and husband Ricardo Calderon. They manage a few different plots of land around the mill where they've planted a mix of cultivars such as Catuaí, Gesha, and the SL-28 bourbon variety from Kenya. Quality is at the front of the Castillo-Calderon family who put a lot of care and intention in their farm and post-harvest practices, which has earned them top placement in past Cup of Excellence competitions. The coffee is grown between 1800 and 2000 meters above sea level. This lot is a separation of Catuaí cultivar, processed using the traditional wet process/"White Honey" method. This differs from typical wet processing because there is no fermentation involved to remove the sticky mucilage layer. Instead, they use a mechanical demucilager to remove most of the fruit, and then a clean-water soak before drying on raised drying tables. While you should expect some chaff during roasting, there's quite a bit less than honey process, and more uniform coloring too.

name: Costa Rica Tarrazú El Mango
short_description: Simple and restrained, El Mango fits the bill of a "daily driver" coffee at a range of roast levels . Notes of milk chocolate, almond, Snickerdoodle cookie, black tea, apple, cocoa, mild acidity. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: While I'm a fan of fruity flavors, it's often the simple, restrained coffees I prefer for my daily brew - coffees like El Mango. The dry fragrance possessed a scent of rapidura-type dark sugar, with dark cocoa and nut. Pouring hot water on the grounds brought out a note of oatmeal cookies made with brown sugar, along with hints of chocolate milk chocolate, and marzipan. In the cup, I found light roasts displaying well-developed sweetness (City/City+), with notes of brown sugar and caramelized sugars, along with bittersweet accents and a hint of apple base note, fading to hints of apple. There's a hint of cinnamon spice in lighter roasts that brought to mind Snickerdoodle cookies, adding a pleasant dimension to the aroma. My Full City roast really brought out the low-toned cup flavors, like semi-sweet chocolate chips, 70% dark chocolate bar, and hot chocolate. It has milder acidity than some of our other Costa Rican coffees, making it a good candidate for espresso too.
farm_notes: This coffee comes from a farmer named Cesar Esquivel in Costa Rica's famed Tarrazú growing region. This particular lot is from a small plot called "El Mango", named for the fruit trees that are also planted here. It's a mechanically washed, which means that instead of using fermentation to remove the sticky fruit after depulping, they strip both cherry and fruit away using what's called a mechanical demucilager. It's the same machinery used to produce honey process coffee too. A simple adjustment to the demucilager affects how much fruit is left intact after depulping. The amount of fruit left intact often correlates to the color change as it dries, which is how they came up with names like "yellow", "red", and even "black honey". This lot was processed as what's referred to as "White Honey" in Costa Rica because there's so little fruit that you can see the white parchment layer that surrounds the seed. It's a close approximation to "fully washed", fermented coffee, with clean cup flavors, and acidity that sparkles. There is a bit more chaff produced during roasting than a fully washed coffee, but nowhere near the amount of dry process or honey process coffees. The coffee also presents darker during the roasting process, which is something to pay attention to when judging roast level, as they are often slightly lighter than they appear. The city of San Marcos is in the Talamanca Sierra highlands, with peaks reaching as high as 3000 meters. It's an ideal micro-region and climate for growing coffee with rich volcanic soil, great altitude, and is shaded from the hot afternoon suns by mountain peaks. The farms surrounding the Cerro La Cruz mill top out around 1900 meters above sea level.

name: Costa Rica Tarrazu La Casona
short_description: Brightly sweet Costa Rica profile, mouth cleansing flavors, molasses, honey graham, barley tea, apple-like acidity, lighter body, nuanced finishing notes of lemon rind and tannic tea. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: This lot La Casona micromill has dark sugars in the cup, and nuanced finishing flavors that come to a point. At City roast level, the dry fragrance has a scent of raw sugar, honey wheat puff cereal, and herbal tea. The wet grounds offer up light caramels and butter toffee, with more of the tea-like hints in the background. City and City+ brews present balanced sweetness in the cup, with lighter body, and acidity that comes off malic and apple-like. Sweetness of molasses and honey graham cracker construct a convincing base flavor, fading to an ever so slightly to lemon rind bittering and barley tea, with mouth-cleansing tannic notes in the aftertaste. It brews a brightly sweet washed Costa Rica flavor profile at lighter roast levels, mouth cleansing flavors, contrasted by light cocoa accents. I enjoyed the bittersweet flavors in my Full City roast as brewed coffee, but body doesn't quite rise to the occasion for espresso in my opinion.
farm_notes: This microlot is a blend of coffees from the various plots managed by the Solis family at their La Casona micromill in Tarrazu. This particular lot is mechanically washed, which means that in stead of using fermentation to remove the sticky fruit after depulping, they strip both cherry and fruit away using a mechanical demucilager equipment. It's the same machinery used to produce honeys. A simple adjustment to the demucilager affects how much fruit is left intact after depulping. The more fruit, the wilder the cup flavors. This lot was processed as what's referred to as "White Honey", which just means they remove as much fruit as possible without scoring the seed. The resulting cup is a close approximation to "fully washed", fermented coffee, with clean cup flavors, and acidity that sparkles. There is a bit more chaff produced during roasting than a fully washed coffee, but nowhere near the amount of dry process or honey process coffees. The city of San Marcos is in the Talamanca Sierra highlands, with peaks reaching as high as 3000 meters. It's an ideal micro-region and climate for growing coffee with rich volcanic soil, great altitude, and is shaded from the hot afternoon suns by mountain peaks. The farms surrounding the La Casona mill top out at 1900 meters above sea level.

name: Costa Rica Yellow Honey Helsar de Zarcero
short_description: Balanced sweetness, silky body and moderate bright accents. Syrupy texture is punctuated by a flavor of chocolate sauce, with accents of toasted coconut, almond, apple and a spiced finish. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: This Helsar lot has a classic Costa Rica profile of balanced sweetness and chocolate roast flavors, silky body and a moderate 'pop' of acidity that brings some structure to the profile. The grinds offer a hint of honey in the sweetness with faint fruited dimension, along with a walnut note. Dark sugars mark the wet aroma, especially in the City-City+ range, with a cinnamon-laced honey note and wisps of cocoa powder. This coffee is so nice to drink, sweet-to-bittering flavors are harmonious at medium roast levels, with faint top notes that emerge as the coffee cools. Body is syrupy, punctuated by a flavor note of chocolate sauce, the roast flavors leading into accents of toasted coconut and almond. I pick out a bit of baking spice/cinnamon powder in the aroma that pairs well with an apple-like acidic note. Full City roasts are very chocolaty and thick-bodied, with complex bittersweet notes of bean to bar chocolates, and a spiced finish.
farm_notes: The Helsar de Zarcero mill represents the efforts of Ricardo Perez Barrantes, whose farms and mill are on a high ridge in the area of Alajuela, in the coffee areas of both Zarcero and Naranjo. This area is renowned for coffee production, but not every farmer has the milling machinery to process coffee down to the green seed. Ricardo saw a need for building one of his own, a small local mill where he could process his coffee, and that of his neighbors. He was one of the first in the region to build out a "micro mill", a term that would soon become synonymous with Costa Rican coffee. This might sound like an obvious move, but it was really revolutionary for Costa Rica, where large volumes had traditionally been the focus. Micro mills helped usher in the shift to producing smaller lots that represent single farms and local towns, rather than full container blends. This lot is a small blend of a few producers next to the Helsar mill. It's a mix of Caturra and Catuaí, grown between 1500 and 1750 meters above sea level. Helsar uses forced demucilage equipment to machine-wash their coffee, an efficient method with low environmental impact that has similar outcomes to traditional wet-fermentation processing.

name: Costa Rica Zarcero Monte Brisas Danto
short_description: Balanced bittersweetness, hints of burnt caramel, citrus zest, dried raisin, marzipan, chocolate-toned bass flavors when roasted dark, full body, baking chocolate in the finish. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Pungent roast tones in the ground coffee are tempered by subtly sweet accents at City+, with hints of raw sugars, dark cocoa powder, and hazelnut. The aroma draws out a mildly sweet scent of dried hibiscus, brown sugar, and hints of dried fruit and malted cocoa. The cup produced convincing sweetness and very nice body, a chocolate-toned bass flavor augmented by notes of burnt caramel, sorghum syrup, and molasses cookie. There's a pleasant shimmer of acidity at City/City+ that shows a malic/apple-like impression, and tartly-sweet. Full City pushes the dark flavors to the forefront, and a bit more heavy-handed; dark chocolate brownie, tangy cacao nibs, with bittering baking chocolate wafers in the aftertaste. This is going to make a great single origin espresso in the Full City-Full City+ range.
farm_notes: Maria Elena Castro and son Luis Salazar opened their micro mill, Beneficio Monte Brisas, back in 2011 after years of delivering their coffee cherry to other mills and cooperatives. Maria Elena's farm, Finca Danto, sits at 1750 meters above sea level on the lush mountainous slopes of Zarcero in Costa Rica's famed West Valley growing region. The Pacific is the major influence in the West Valley with sprawling views of Naranjo and Alajuela readily available across it. This is a separation of Centroamericano, which is what's called a first generation hybrid, in this case using a Timor Hybrid and Ethiopian Rume Sudan. It has some disease resistence, high yield, and great cup potential - especially when grown at high altitudes. The Monte Brisas mill is incredibly clean and well cared for, and feels a bit like a museum with all of its meticulously maintained older machinery! The coffee is mechanically washed on a Desacafe machine and sun dried on raised beds adjacent to the wet mill. Leaving that fruit mucilage intact instead of washing it away is the hallmark of honey process coffee. This lot, however, is what some call "semi-washed", or "white honey", which is the Costa Rican equivalent of a fully washed coffee. The demucilager machine is calibrated to remove as much fruit as possible. Then the coffee is soaked for a short period to help wash away some of the remaining fruit. Without fermentation, there is still a very thin layer of fruit intact. This means the coffee looks a little darker when roasting it, and a much higher instance of chaff than the typical fully washed/fermented coffee.

name: El Salvador Dry Process Miravalles Pacamara
appearance: .4 d/300gr, 15+ Screen - a range of sizes up to around 18/19 screen
short_description: A more fruit-forward, bittersweet profile than the washed Pacamara we sold earlier this year. Intense roast tones, burnt sugar, layered dark cocoa, rustic dried fruits and winey accents, lemon sage aroma, lime zest. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: This dry process Pacamara from Miravalles has more of a fruit-forward, bittersweet profile than the washed lot we sold earlier this year. From the grounds to the wet aroma, we picked up on notes of dried berry and stone fruit, with rustic sweeteners of molasses and palm sugars, and bittersweet cocoa. The cup has very nice intensity, City/City+ roasts producing pungent roast tones of burnt sugars, with layers of dark cocoa that balance out potent fruits and herbal accents. The cup cools to hints of mixed berry jam, plum wine and a bit of dried prune. There's an herbal/citrus element to the aroma that draws out some complex notes of zested lime and a hint of lemon sage in the nose. Bittersweetness comes through at all roast levels, particularly pronounced at Full City and darker. Dark cacao notes are front and center, a bittersweet sharpness that fades to rustic dried date in the finish. It's fairly complex for Salvadoran coffee, and a good demonstration of how the dry process method impacts cup flavors.
farm_notes: Pacamara is a hybrid cultivar of Pacas (natural mutation of Bourbon), and Maragogype. They're perhaps most well known for their large size, however this lot ranges in size from somethign similar to standard Bourbon (around 15/16") up to the larger end of Pacamara (around 19/64"). This dry process is a much more fruit-forward coffee than the wet process counterpart we also purchased, also capable of dark toned bittersweetness when roasted to the medium-dark range. The coffee comes from the Miravalles farm in Ahuachapan, a 120 manzanas farm that is planted in many different varieties, including a small amount of Pacamara. Finca Miravalles is a family affair. It's owned by husband and wife Luis Duarte and Tete Chacón, and much of the management is handled by their son, Luis Jr, and Chico, the on-site manager of 15 years. The farm is located in Apaneca, Ahuachapan, not too far from the Santa Ana volcano. It used to be two separate farms, Miravalles belonging to Tete's family, Santa Maria to Luis's. They were both raised on these neighboring farms, family ownership going back some 150 years. Sometime after marrying, they put in an offer on Miravalles, which was all but abandoned at the time, and joined with Santa Maria under the Miravalles name. They have been renovating the farm ever since, keeping much of the original Bourbon and Pacas cultivars, and planting several other varieties, including H1 and F1 hybrids, Catimor, Pacamara, Caturra, and Gesha. They've done an amazing job segregating the cultivars in separate plots, and go to great lenghts to harvest and process separately too. Miravalles is perched on the verdant slopes of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec mountain region, and spans an altitude range of about 1250 to 1550 meters above sea level. Check out our video tour of the Miravalles farm , and in-depth look at their wet process method in action at their mill.

name: El Salvador Miravalles Pacamara
appearance: .2 d/300gr, 15+ Screen - a range of sizes up to around 18/19 screen
short_description: A nice counterpoint to some of the more low-toned Salvadoran coffees, with nuanced top notes, round sweetness, and moderate level of acidity. Dark sugar, date, chocolate orange, plum, herbal hints, cornsilk tea. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: This Pacamara lot from the Miravalles farm offers a nice counterpoint to some of the more low-toned Salvadoran coffees. It brings nuanced top notes to a caramely undertone, with a touch more acidity too. The fragrance of the dry grounds had a lightly fruited sweetness, bran muffin with raisin, brown sugar, and a touch of herbal spice tea. The wet aroma is a bit more potent, honey and raw sugar, with some zested lime, and a hint of cooked fruit. The cup shows a convincing level of sweetness, with round body pulls at some of the fruited threads that make a mild impression in the cup. Dark sugars and balanced roast flavors provide a nice base layer, accented by hints of plum and deried date, with an aromatic herbal note, and a bright spot of cornsilk tea. My darkest roast hit Full City, a bit darker than I'd normally take a complex coffee like this. The sweetness was still very impressive, hinting at profiles of burnt caramel, raisin, and chocolate orange. While Pacamara's tend to skew large, this lot has a range of sizes. We buy all of the 15 screen and up (measured in 15/64") in order to maximize the lot size. This year's harvest was much bigger than last, and we were able to secure 20 bags wet process, and 18 bags of a dry process lot that will come later this Summer.
farm_notes: Pacamara is a hybrid cultivar of Pacas (natural mutation of Bourbon), and Maragogype. They're perhaps most well known for their large size, however this lot ranges in size from somethign similar to standard Bourbon (around 15/16") up to the larger end of Pacamara (around 19/64"). It comes from the Miravalles farm in Ahuachapan, a 120 manzanas farm that is planted in many different varieties, including a small amount of Pacamara. Finca Miravalles is a family affair. It's owned by husband and wife Luis Duarte and Tete Chacón, and much of the management is handled by their son, Luis Jr, and Chico, the on-site manager of 15 years. The farm is located in Apaneca, Ahuachapan, not too far from the Santa Ana volcano. It used to be two separate farms, Miravalles belonging to Tete's family, Santa Maria to Luis's. They were both raised on these neighboring farms, family ownership going back some 150 years. Sometime after marrying, they put in an offer on Miravalles, which was all but abandoned at the time, and joined with Santa Maria under the Miravalles name. They have been renovating the farm ever since, keeping much of the original Bourbon and Pacas cultivars, and planting several other varieties, including H1 and F1 hybrids, Catimor, Pacamara, Caturra, and Gesha. They've done an amazing job segregating the cultivars in separate plots, and go to great lenghts to harvest and process separately too. Miravalles is perched on the verdant slopes of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec mountain region, and spans an altitude range of about 1250 to 1550 meters above sea level. Check out our video tour of the Miravalles farm, and in-depth look at their wet process method in action at their mill.

name: Ethiopia Dry Process Birbirsa
short_description: Brightly-accented dry process coffee, with stone fruit and honey notes that are unique to coffees from the West. Red honey, pear, peach, Earl Grey tea, cocoa bittersweets (especially in dark roasts). City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: We are pleased to once again offer this impressive dry process lot from Birbirsa coop in Western Jimma. The dry fragrance was lightly fruited across our roast range, hints of stone fruit with honey and brown sugar. The wet aroma showed more bountiful fruit notes, but still had a lighter, wet process intensity than some of our other dry process coffees. Hints of dried peach, lime, citrus tea, came through, along with a honey sweetness that hangs in the air. These roasts brewed bright fruited flavors for dry process coffee, with stone fruit and citrus highlights, similar to some of the other Western Ethiopian coffees we buy. Sipping a City roast, flavor profiles included juicy flavors of pear and peach, dried apricot, and an orange marmalade note. It has a very nice acidic dimension for dry process coffee, tea-like, that along with spice hints in the cup aroma, brings out notes of Earl Grey tea with lemon. Honey sweetness is syrupy, fading to some really nice roast flavors of cocoa bittering in the aftertaste. At Full City, the vibrance was dulled  a bit, but you're left with bittersweet chocolate that suits the syrupy texture, along with hints of rustic dried fruits.
farm_notes: The Birbirsa coffee cooperative is located in Beshasha Badiya, Jimma, not far from a few other coops we buy from. It's on the smaller size in comparison, both in terms of physical and membership numbers, with 80 local farmers making up its base. Beshasha town has very good altitude, registering at just under 2100 meters above sea level. It is conveniently situated along the side of one of the main dirt road that runs through town, affording good access for moving coffee on and off the site. As a matter of fact, we made an unplanned visit to Birbirsa in 2019 on our way to another coop. The colorful sign, and colorfully dressed manager Mohammed, drew us in like a beacon on the side of the dusty road (that's Mohammed in the beautiful green shirt and tie in front of Birbirsa sign). During our tour of the site, we saw that the cherry selection looked great, and have been buying their coffee ever since. They only produce dry process at the moment, which is fine by us considering the quality! They focus on doing one thing, and they do it very well.

name: Ethiopia Dry Process Bobea Uke
short_description: Straddles the line between fruit-forward flavors and delicate aromatics, excellent both light and medium roasted. Berry-toned sweetness, passion fruit, dried peach, tea bittering, whole spices, chocolate-covered fruit. City to Full City. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Bobea Uke lets off a scent of fragrant fruits and milk chocolate in the ground coffee, punctuated by notes of strawberry and dried peach, red honey and light spice accents. The honey sweetness builds intensity in the wetted crust, and smells saturated like baklava pastry, with notes of butterscotch, chocolate-covered dried fruits, and blackberry pie filling. The cup straddles the line between fruit-forward process flavors and delicate aromatics. It's fruited and bright when roasted light, but also capable of producing deeper-toned chocolates and syrupy fruits when roasted dark. At City roast level, flavors are berry-toned and a bit juicy, blackberry and cranberry juice, with hints of dried stone fruits. There's a very nice aromatic overlay to the fruited profile that brings on floral hints, as well as tropical accents of passion fruit and mango. The light roasts carry a moderate level of acidity for dry process coffee, with citrus and berry accents that bring a structured feel to the complex array of flavors. The finish has a pungent bittering side, like tannic black tea, fading to hints of whole spices. Full City was a surprise hit for us too, dark-toned and juicy, with profiles of chocolate-covered berry, grape, and a powdery cocoa note in the long finish. It made an excellent fruit-forward espresso, berry-laden cocoa, apricot nectar, with some grabby orange zest in the aftertaste.
farm_notes: Bobea Uke processing site serves roughly 1200 small holder coffee farmers in Woreda Odo Shakiso, Western Guji. Elevation at the site is roughly 2000 meters above sea level, and the farms they buy cherry from range from 1850 to 2250 meters above sea level. Each lot they produce is made up of coffee from hundreds of different farmers in the region, most with only a few hundred coffee trees or less. You tend to see coffee intercropped with other fruits and vegetables, "false banana" being one the more common food staples to see planted in the region. The false banana plant has many uses, and is widely utilized for it's starchy inners that are often fermented with yeast to make a bread ("kocho"), and the leaves can be transformed into roofs for houses, baskets, and more. Bobea coffee station is a privately run operation and they only produce dry process coffees at this time. Dry processing is the oldest processing method and involves drying the coffee bean and cherry whole. From pictures you see, you might think you can just dump the cherries to the beds and wait. This is not the case! The coffee has to be spread out to a layer depth of only a few centimeters, no more, in order to allow air flow. The coffee is turned hourly, or even more frequently, in order to facilitate even drying and keep the coffee from molding. It's not difficult, but requires constant attention. During this time of physical attention, workers continually pull out lower quality coffee in the form of physical defects and coffee that was not harvested at peak ripeness. This lot underwent several layers of hand picking from the whole coffee cherry to the final milled green coffee in order to achieve "Grade 1" status.

name: Ethiopia Dry Process Guji Goro
short_description: Pairs dry process flavors of expressive fruits and rustic sweetness with the kind of bright acidity and aromatic highlights of a washed coffee . Boysenberry, dried apricot, potpourri, citrus, chocolate-covered fruit. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: Guji Goro pairs potent dry process flavors of intense fruits and rustic sweetness with the kind of bright acidity and aromatic highlights that are much more in line with washed coffee. The dry fragrance is peppered with berry notes, both dried and cooked, accented by hints of rustic sugars around the edges. The berry aspects really come through in the wet aroma, with a potent cooked blackberry note, like a berry compote, along with a spice note that brought up some cinnamon streusel for me. At City/City+ level, the brewed coffee offers fragrant fruit and berry notes, unrefined sugars, with dried blueberry and tannic tea in the finish. An aromatic overlay is redolent with fruit accents of boysenberry, blackberry juice and dried apricot, along with suggestions of dried potpourri and herbal rue leaf. The profile is expressive and complex, and the light roasts offer vibrant acidity that brings up Rose's lime, with bittering rind in the aftertaste. Faint rustic notes are true to the process method, like notes of sorghum and rice syrup sweeteners, preserved lemon and fragrant palo santo sticks. Full City roasts consolidate deep chocolate tones with juicy berry accents, and have tactile appeal on the palate. The acidity level is blunted quite a bit in the dark roasts, but you're left with a composite of dark chocolate and dried berry that's truly delicious.
farm_notes: This dry process lot is from Goro station, located just a short jaunt from Hambela Wamena, where a good portion of our Guji coffee comes from. The site sits at around 2100 meters above sea level, with coffee planted between 1900 and 2300 meters. These lots are made up from the coffees of hundreds of local farmers who have very small plots of coffee, most with less than 2 hectares of planted land. Farmers deliver their coffee to stations like Goro, where it is bought as ripe cherry, and then processed down to the green seed. This is a dry process coffee, but Goro also has a wet mill for wet proces coffee too. For dry process coffee, they sort out as much of the unripe coffee as they can before sending to the drying tables where it takes 2-3 weeks to dry. We visited several stations run by this group, however Goro was not one of them. Their stations are all very well organized, both in terms of tracking payments to he farmers they buy from, and in their reinvestment in maintaining their processing equipment and drying beds. They also promote sustainable farming methods to the farmers they buy from, like tree stumping, organic compost, and not using fungicides on the coffee trees.

name: Ethiopia Dry Process Kercha Haruse
short_description: On the "light and bright" end of the spectrum for dry process coffees, clean fresh fruits, citron essence, yuzu, and mandarin, lightly floral, fragrant black tea. Makes an excellent pour-over brew. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: City roasts of Haruse smelled amazing, and the flavors in the cup followed suit. While this brews delicious fruit top notes, it's more on the "light and bright" end of the spectrum of dry process coffee flavors. Grinding the coffee left a sweet honey scent hanging in the air, potent and almost floral in sweetness, with accents of golden apricot and peach pie filling. The wet aroma was peppered with sweet, floral fruits, like peach blossom, fresh apricot, and mango, and the steam smelled saturated with light brown sugars. The brew is bright and very aromatic, and I found it to have a lot in common with wet process coffees. Fruits have a freshness to them, like fragrant citrus types such as mandarin orange, yuzu, and citron essence. The cup sweetness is not sacrificed in light roasts either, with notes of demerara and sucanat raw sugars propping up some of the more delicate flavors. The aroma has a perfumed quality to it as it cools, with elegant floral hints of honeysuckle, and sweet freesia flowers in the nose, along with fragrant black teas. In general, we found Haruse to be ideal for a fragrant pour-over brew, highlighting the clean sweetness and cup aroma, as well as a bright and syrupy body that's on the lighter, silky side.
farm_notes: This coffee is from a site near Kercha town, close to the border of Uraga in Ethiopia's southern Guji Zone. It's from a privately owned station who have an outgrower program with more than 1500 Guji farmers, whose coffee they buy, process, and export. In practice, this essentially means the mill owner is supplying small holders with seedlings, and often agronomical support as well, in order to promote coffee production in the regions they operate in. The family who owns the mill has 150,000 hectares of coffee too, and makes up a chunk of their exportable volume each year. There were many reasons to be drawn to their Haruse lot this season, with clean cup flavors topping the list. It shares a lot in common with washed coffee ("wet process"), especially in the brighter citrus notes and aromatic floral overlay that comes through when roasted in the City-City+ range. Most of the farmers who sell to Haruse have less than 1 hectare of coffee, and the farms reach as high as 2,200 meters above sea level in the region.

name: Ethiopia Duromina Aba Bulgu
short_description: Syrupy honey sweetness is brightly accented by aromatic fruits and vibrant citrus notes. Accents of juicy stone fruits, ripe strawberry, mango, lemon Italian ice, hibiscus tea. Works well at a range of roast levels. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: I think this is the third year we've bought coffee from Aba Bulgu, but we've only purchased his dry process coffee up until now. This year, we were able to procure two lots from this Jimma producer, both natural and washed. If you've tasted coffee from Duromina cooperative, the cup flavors found here should be familiar. It has the kind of honeyed sweetness and stone fruit-floral qualities that are unique to coffees from this Western region. The grinds let off a scent of malt syrup and peach, with a zesty lime accent, and floral hint. "Warm honey", was what came to mind when pouring the hot water, a potent level of sweetness, with aromatic accents of orange blossom, dried stone fruit, and bright, tea-like notes. At City roast level, the cup is brightly accented by aromatic fruits and vibrant citrus notes, peach that's reached a floral-level of ripeness, strawberry, hibiscus and apricot teas, lemon Italian ice and a hint of mango. Notes of red honey and fruit-flavored syrups give this coffee an appealing syrupy quality, and the acidity toes the line between tartaric and citric, underscored by an array of fruit accents. We were very happy with how it cupped at Full City level too, more on the roast-toned chocolate side of the flavor spectrum, but with hints of juicy black plum, orange rind and toasted coconut in the aftertaste.
farm_notes: This coffee is from a farmer named Abdurhiman Aba Bulgu in Kedamesa, which is part of Woreda Goma. In fact, his farm is a part of the Duromina area, a name you likely recognize as being linked to a cooperative of the same name. Aba Bulgu ("Aba" is a term of reverence that translates to "father") has an 13 hectare farm and produces both wet and dry process coffee, this being the former. We've bought his excellent dry process coffee in previous years, but this is the first washed coffee we've tried, and it's very nice! The altitude at Aba Bulgu's farm spans 1975 to 2200 meters above sea level, and planted primarily in a variety from the Jimma Agricultural Research Center ("JARC"), simply identified as "74110". JARC is the government coffee research center, and responsible for breeding improved sub varieties from many of the heirloom local coffee strains. Currently, there are 42 different JARC types, and 74110 is a fairly common one to see planted, along with others, like 74112.

name: Ethiopia Guji Hambela Dabaye
short_description: Delicious and delicate light roasted, refined sweetness, tart acidity, and fragrant accents. Notes of honey, simple syrup, maple, pear, orange marmalade, and floral hints that permeate the aroma. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: Delicious and delicate, this wet-processed lot from Hambela Dabaye delivers impressive sweetness, with bright fruits and aromatic accents in the City-City+ roast range. The dry grounds smelled of fragrant white honey and burnt sugar, light hints of berry juice, and ginger tea. A more intense aromatic profile emerges from the wetted grounds, and running my spoon through the coffee crust releases a potent mix of raw sugars, honey, with syrupy pear, and floral tea. Our City roast produced mouth-cleansing flavors, refined and a bit juicy, with aromatic grace notes that play off pronounced sweetness underneath. The cup sweetness has layers of simple syrup, maple, and a fragrant white honey note in the finish. As the coffee cools down some, I pick up on more of the fruited flavors like nectarine, orange marmalade, and pear, along with perfumed floral highlights, like jasmine and rose water. The acidic impression has elements of tart citrus that are well integrated into the sweetness. Much of the coffee character can be described as light and delicate, and you should give it a light treatment in the roaster too. Pulling 1 minute and 30 seconds after the start of 1st Crack is not too soon! The coffee coloring might look slightly mottled and uneven, but it's where we've found some of the liveliest pour-over brews.
farm_notes: Hambela Dabaye is from longtime Guji coffee farmer and mill manager, Kedir Hassan. He is the older brother to Esmael Hassan, who you may remember as the producer of another Guji coffee we've also carried, Kayon Mountain. "Dabaye" is the name of the kebele where this Hambela station is located (a town, more or less). We were lucky enough to be hosted at this station on our December 2018 visit, camping out in a pair of military tents replete with cots, overlooking the couple hundred drying tables below us. Kedir is an incredibly proficient and capable engineer as well as coffee farmer, and built the entire Hambela station in one season. You wouldn't know this, as it's visually apparent everything was built with high processing standards, and with efficiency in mind. Of course he did not complete Hambela on his own, and thanks to his long standing connection with the the people in this area, he had much needed community support. Hambela sits at 1816 meters above sea level, and coffee is grown as high as 2100 meters. They mostly buy coffee from farmers in the surrounding kebeles of Buliye, Wamena, Borticha, Dari Rogicha and Dabaye, of course. The mill is also certified organic, though we did not buy this lot with a certificate.

name: Ethiopia Uraga Raro Boda
short_description: Light and bright coffee, tea-like and aromatic. It pulls out delicate sweetness and mouth cleansing acidity, with notes Earl Grey, jasmine, lemongrass, basil, simple syrup, honey and limeade. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: At City roast level, Raro Boda is a light and bright brewed coffee, tea-like and aromatic. It pulls out delicate sweetness and mouth cleansing acidity too that makes for quite a compelling pour-over. I dropped my roast 1:25 after the start of 1st Crack and was surprised by the level of sweetness in the cup. The fragrance and aroma are potent with fragrant notes of semi-refined sugars and loose leaf black tea, a hint of floral jasmine and fruit accents, like citrus and grape. Pouring hot water on the grounds lifted citrus-accented sweetness, white honey, orange, with notes of baking spices mixed in. The brewed coffee starts off with transparent flavors of simple syrup, opening up to a sort of light orange blossom honey note that held on in the aftertaste. The cup gives off an intoxicating aromatic profile, star jasmine is in there like always, but it's the tea-like notes that really front and center. Flavors of Earl Grey tea, bergamot citrus, and perfumed lemongrass tea were noted, as well as herbal accents of rue and sweet basil. The acidity is bright on the palate, with fragrant lemon and limeade notes lending a refreshing sharpness to the profile. City+ brews were a little less bright, but had a tannic quality, like long-steeped black tea, that added a bittering dimension to the acidic impression.
farm_notes: Raro Boda washing station is located in the village of Raro Boda, on the eastern edge of Uraga, a name quickly becoming well known for regional cup quality. This particular site buys from around 700 small scale farmers in the area, each with less than 1 hectare of coffee planted on average. Raro Boda was established in 2018, and they've continued to invest in wet processing equipment in an effort to improve quality and efficiency. They recently replaced all of their fermentation tanks with ceramic material which is much easier to keep clean than cement. Raro Boda coffee is collected from very high altitudes surrounding the station, up to 2250 meters above sea level! They produce both wet and dry process coffee, and we were really taken by the clean cup, and floral character of this particular lot.

name: Ethiopia Uraga SWP Decaf
appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 14-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination
short_description: Lively decaf coffee, sweetness that's fairly refined, like simple syrup made with brown sugar. Notes of honey, lemon black tea, chocolate malted grain, cherry cordial, and lemongrass in the nose. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: The ground coffee had very nice sweetness in both our City, and Full City roasts. The lighter of the two had a note of spiced sugars, like a mixture of demerara raw sugar and cinnamon powder, complex and fragrant, and definitely not typical decaf. In the wet aroma, a red honey note imbued the steam with sweetness, along with a scent of baked apple with brown sugar and cinnamon, and honey wheat bread. The cup acidity is apparent when the coffee is hot, like black tea with a twist of lemon, bright and refreshing. It helps give the cup a really nice "washed" character - that is to say the clean, bright cup characteristics of a wet process Ethiopian coffee (which it was made from). City roasts had refined sweetness of simple syrup made with brown sugar, accented by notes of honey, and fragrant lemongrass in the nose. As it cooled down some, I picked up on some notes of chocolate malted grains, likely a bi-product of decaffeination, but totally pleasant nonetheless! The cup sweetness holds up at Full City too, roast-toned like semi-sweet dark chocolate (think Hershey's Dark), and offers a mild fruit tone of cherry cordial, with some more bittering cacao nibs in the aftertaste. It's a medium body coffee, which carries the flavor profile quite well, but perhaps a little too thin for espresso.
farm_notes: The Uraga Woreda is home to some of the highest altitude coffees we buy, many of the farms topping out at 2300 meters above sea level. Altitude plays a role in coffee density, the higher altitude zones slowing rates of maturation, which in turn produces a much denser coffee with higher potential for sweetness and acidity. Most of the coffee in this custom decaf was sourced from two separate Uraga wet mills, Gogogu and Haro, whose consistently produce high quality coffees that are sweetly aromatic and clean. I found this decaf relatively easy to roast, 1st crack being much louder than some other decafs we've had, and the surface color fairly even (light roasts too). I should mention that there are some small beans in the mix (likely as small as 14 screen), and Behmor users should give the wire grid drum a shake to let loose the occasional bean that slip through the screen. This coffee was processed by Swiss Water Decaf in Vancouver, BC whose chemical-free method only uses water (well, "water, temperature, and time" as you'll see on their website) to remove 99.9% of the caffeine. In terms of decaffeination, it's one of the gentler processes on the coffee and helps retain much of the coffees original flavor. In this case, the decaf brings impressive wet process Ethiopian flavors that are dynamic, sweet, and aromatic.

name: Flores Dry Process Manggarai Colol Robusta
short_description: Nice Robusta example, but still aggressive and intensely bitter. Unsweetened baking chocolate, toasted grain, pungent whole spice, muted sweetness, low acidity, very thick body. Full City to French. Good for milk drinks.
full_cupping_notes: There's nothing quite like Robusta coffee, an important detail to clarify from the drop. If you've tried it before and are back for more, you can skip this part, but all others take note! What typical Robusta coffee lacks in sweetness, it makes up for in intense bittering flavors and body. It is low in acidity, and high in caffeine content, making it a popular choice for dark roasted commercial blends. This is not "typical" Robusta, however. It was grown at high altitude, processed with quality in mind, and it shows. It is still incredibly intense, bittering at its core, but the mild top notes and subtle sweetness that make it so drinkable are a testament to the quality-focused efforts of this group. The fragrance and aroma at Full City/Full City+ had a scent of unsweetened cocoa (like Baker's brand), laced with savory toasted grain, and a very slight hint of fruit. I picked up on very subtle sweetness too, and accents of whole spices. The cup came off quite similar, very bitter chocolate, brothy sweetness, cooked barley, coriander, star anise, and lingering finish. Full City+ roasts had a pungent clove note that paired well with the punchy roast bittering. Single origin shots are too intense for my taste, but I think some will enjoy it under a pillow of milk. Body is seriously as thick as it gets for coffee - think heavy whipping cream - and flavors are roasted cacao nibs, leather, mesquite, and a hint of clove in the aftertaste. It would make a really nice blend base. A comment on roasting: First crack isn't very audible. We noticed occasional 'pops', but it's not clearly defined like most coffee. The fracturing of first crack is easy to spot and can be monitored that way if you have visual access while roasting. Second crack, however, is much more pronounced, and honestly the preferred roast target for me.
farm_notes: If you've never tasted it before, Robusta can be quite a shock. I's a distinct species of coffee altogether ("Coffea Canephora") unrelated to Arabica, known for robust physical characteristics, high productivity, and resilience to disease and fungus. In terms of the cup, Robusta is characterized by intense bittering flavors, thick body, and low acidity. This, in conjunction with a high caffeine content, are what makes it such an attractive option for dark roasted commercial blends. There's been a push in recent years to produce "Specialty Robusta", both as a way of adding value to an historically undervalued crop, and also as an alternative revenue source in areas where Arabica is harder to produce. This lot comes from a quality focused effort in Flores, where a small network of Robusta collectors work with neighboring farms in Colol Village to improve harvest and post harvest practices in service of the cup. This lot was the top scoring Robusta from the harvest, and we found it to have a lot more going on than just bittering intensity, like subtle sweet notes, and whole spices. It's still very intense, and nothing like any other coffee on our list. But it's an interesting example of the direction some Robusta growers are taking, showing that by treating their Robusta crops with the care and attention they would Arabica, it makes a positive impact on the cup. A comment on roasting: First crack isn't very audible. We noticed occasional 'pops', but it's not clearly defined like most coffee. The fracturing of first crack is easy to spot and can be monitored that way if you have visual access while roasting. Second crack, however, is much more pronounced, and honestly the preferred roast target for me.

name: Guatemala Antigua Finca San Miguel Urias
short_description: Flavors are familiar and simple, well-balanced and easy to drink. Malty-sweetness, burnt sugar, almond, milk chocolate and mild hint of acidity. It's the kind of coffee I find myself reaching for. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Balanced coffees are much harder to talk about than those with outlier flavors, but more often than not, they're the coffees we find ourselves reaching for. San Miguel Urias is one of those coffees. It's not overly anything. Rather, simplicity is its strength and it's very easy to drink! This is the main reason it was used as the control sample for the recent "Fermentation Project" global cupping hosted by Lucia Solis and James Hoffman. It provided the perfect reference point to return to in order to pick out subtle differences that were a bi-product of the multiple methods of wet processing used for the experiment. The coffee for this review was roasted to about City+, which roughly correlates to 13% moisture loss after roasting. The fragrance and aroma had a scent of minimally processed sugars, molasses and faint nutty hints. When brewed, the cup sweetness sits in a nice place with acidity, and subtle top notes offer soft contrast without taking over the cup. When hot, there's a malty aspect to the sweetness, like malt syrup with accents of Horlicks malted milk, and some burnt sugar in the aftertaste. A background bittersweet note brought to mind milk chocolate, and a mild acidic impression suggests apple and maybe a hint of tea.
farm_notes: This coffee comes from Finca San Miguel Urias, whose farm and mill straddle the edge of Antigua town, not far from Ciudad Vieja. The farm is planted  primarily in Caturra variety, a natural dwarf mutation of Bourbon, along with smaller amounts of H1 and Bourbon. This lot was part of the Fermentation Project global tasting kit, a project put together by fermentation specialist Lucia Solis, and coffee coffee James Hoffmann to examine the impact of fermentation on what we experience in the cup. For the Project, the same coffee lot was harvested and processed in parallel, but utilizing different fermentation approaches in order to understand their influence on flavor. This coffee was the mechanically demucilaged ("machine washed") control, which in many ways served as the somewhat neutral reference point to the three types of fermentations performed with the other three. The process involves pulping the cherry and fruit mucilage in one fell swoop, then sending the coffee straight to the drying patio. The mechanical demucilage process uses very little water compared to traditional wet processing, so you often see this type of wet mill in areas with water scarcity, like Tanzania. Efficiency, and the ability to control how much fruit is left on the seed (if any), also make it a popular choice for mills that produce a lot of honeys, like Costa Rica.

name: Guatemala Antigua La Folie
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Typica Types
short_description: Good cup clarity, bracing highlights and a sweet, refined finish. Notes of cane sugar, marzipan, tangerine, rose hips, with cocoa undertones that can be developed with roast. City to Full City+.
full_cupping_notes: At City to City+ roast level, the dry fragrance is accented by sweet smells of golden honey and cane sugar, with a note of granola with dried apple. The wetted grounds offer a more aromatic sweetness, with notes of buttercream frosting, vanilla bean, and fruit crumble. In the cup, light roasts are pleasantly bracing, with layered sweetness of cane sugar and light muscovado, with an almond-like aromatic hint of marzipan. Folie has the cup clarity that we hope for from Antigua, with bright accents of tangerine and rose hips tea that fade to a very refined finish. At Full City, the mouthfeel is more substantial on the palate and chocolatey, with a bit of caramelized sweetness contributed from the roast taste.
farm_notes: Just outside the town of Antigua is the small village of San Felipe de Jesus. And among the houses on the twisting and narrow side streets is an old coffee farm called La Folie. It is owned by Penny Matheu, having been divided off from the greater Matheu family lands and the neighboring Finca Filadelfia. The farm operates as a small estate of 91 acres. The last time we visited the farm was right after they placed top 5 in the Guatemalan Cup of Excellence competition (despite the fact it was bombarded with rain and mud in a violent storm the day previous). It's a beautiful old-style farm at 1700 meters above sea level, planted chiefly in Bourbon, with Caturra and some Typica as well. The manager, Don Julio Valencia, lived on the farm at that time, and is in some of the photos we have from that visit. The plantings are well-organized in blocks and rows, a classic Antigua style farm on flat, fertile grounds. This is our second lot from La Folie this year, and another prime example of clean wet process Antiguan coffee, with crowd pleasing sweetness, and bright cup character.

name: Guatemala Atitlan Robusta
short_description: Pungent bittering and a potent savory dimension, with thick body and low acidity. Notes of cacao nibs, baking chocolate, burnt popcorn, toasted barley, cumin, long bittering finish. Full City to French. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Robusta are interesting to taste because they taste nothing like Arabica. It has a reputation for intense flavors, pungent bittering and savory notes, low acidity, and very big body. If you've never tried one, you're likely to be shocked! But these characteristics, along with high caffeine content, have made it a regular ingredient in many espresso blends. Finca Panama is a good example of a Robusta prepared to high grade standards. The smells are potent, like roasted cacao nibs, toasty accents of burnt popcorn and wheat puff cereal. The cup is thick in body and flavor, densely packed with robust roast flavors that are dark-toned and chocolatey. This is not a sweet coffee, but it does have lightly-sweet accents of burnt, caramelized sugar and a hint of honey-nut. It's an incredibly deep-toned coffee, pungent with bittering flavors of unsweetened baking chocolate and black cocoa, the finish showing strong flavors of toasted grains, barley/spelt, with savory spices like saffron and cumin, and an incredibly long bittering finish. It's an interesting coffee to taste on its own, and also makes a great bittering/body component in a blend.
farm_notes: This Robusta is from a coffee estate called Finca Panama, in the Atitlán growing region of Guatemala. Finca Panama was established in the 1930's and has experienced many crop changes through the years, but has continually produced coffee. Today, the farm produces coffee, mangosteen, macadamia nuts, natural rubber, bamboo, avocado, lemons and honey. Altitude at the farm spans a range of 800 meters on the low side, all the way up to 1500 meters above sea level. Robusta is a unique coffee species separate from Arabica (which makes up the majority of what we sell, and specialty coffee in general). Unlike Arabica, Robusta can be grown at very low altitudes without the risks of disease, but the tradeoff is lower cup quality. Robusta is known for bitter flavors, big body and flat acidity. Historically, it's traded for much lower prices than Arabica, and a popular choice for blends as a result. In recent years, there's been a push to produce "specialty" grade Robusta, which is what we see here. The same care is put into post harvest practices as what you would expect for a high grade Arabica. That doesn't mean it will taste like the washed Guatemala coffee you're used to! It's an intensely bitter coffee, with unique toasted grain flavors, savory spices and more. They're very interesting coffees to taste, and a little goes a long way in a blend.

name: Guatemala Chimaltenango Tecpán
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids
short_description: Nutty-sweet impressions and bittersweet at a wide range of roasts. Notes of cocoa-dusted almond, toffee nut, chocolate-covered pistachio, cocoa butter and sesame halva. City+ to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: Tecpán gives off nutty-sweet impressions in the cup and is bittersweet across a wide range of roasts. Fruited hints are faint, but do manage to drum up a mild acidic impression. The fragrance and aroma have caramel and walnut, mild milk chocolate and a hint of dried apple. At City+, caramel and cocoa tones are core cup flavors, with nutty-sweet notes of toasted almond and creamy macadamia. Fruits are very low key, but I did pick up on subtle traces of baked apple and bitter citrus peel at this roast level. The finish had a caramel-nut flavor, toffee almond, cocoa butter and sesame halva. Full City roasts are chocolate-toned and richly bittersweet, crip cocoa/nut flavor profiles  come through like cocoa-dusted almonds, and chocolate-covered pistachio. This is a great starting point for espresso, where body is bolstered a bit, and the cocoa-toned flavors have a sharpness that will work great under a pillow of steamed milk.
farm_notes: The city of Tecpán sits in the northwest corner of the Chimaltenango Municipality, about an hour and a half from Guatemala City by car. Tecpán in Nahuatl language means “Mansion of the gods” or “mansion de los dioses” in Spanish, and it was the town of Iximche in Tecpán that was declared the first capital city of Guatemala by the Spanish. It's a very high altitude zone, and known for cold climate, especially at the higher reaches. This region has a median altitude of 2000 meters, which along with the cold climate, means slower coffee cherry maturation and very dense coffee beans. Not always a recipe for a good cup, it certainly helps to have a dense organic structure for sugar caramelization, and Tecpán has proved to be a very sweet, balanced cup. Bourbon and Caturra cultivars are also part of that recipe, the dominant cultivars of the region, and you see smaller amounts of Catuaí, Typica, and Anacafe-90 mixed in too. This coffee is a small producer blend from Tecpán, most farms with much less than 10 hectares of land. The effort is organized by a local farmer named Aurelio Salvador, who has taken charge of buying cherry from those in neighboring villages and coordinating the deliveries to the La Azotea mill on the other side of Chimaltenango, where the coffee is then centrally processed.

name: Guatemala El Socorro Java Variety
short_description: Delicate flavors, transparent sweetness and aromatic top notes are elegant and refined. Great "Java" character, tea-like, lemon, coriander, rose hips, with bracing acidity that suits the light bodied cup. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: This Java cultivar is refined and delicate, with transparent sweetness and aromatic top notes that bring out an elegant side. The fragrance off the dry grounds show a scent of raw sugars laced with toasted barley green tea, vanilla malt and a hint of spice. The sweetness in the wet aroma shows a very nice level of sweetness that comes off like minimally processed sugars, and a wisp of chamomile tea. Java cultivars can be tea-like and delicate, but the cup profile is very tied to roast level. We recommend keeping your roasts to City/City+ if you're looking to highlight those aspects, which roughly correlates to 10-20 degrees F from the start of 1st Crack. If you're roasting on a Behmor, try engaging the cooling cycle 1:00 after the start of 1st Crack and adjust from there. At City roast level the sweetness is transparent, like simple syrup, and underpins the cup with a very nice base flavor. Aromatic accents give the flavors a sense of refinement, with notes of black tea, a squeeze of lemon, rose hips and dried coriander spice. The cup is rounded out by bracing acidity that suits the light body and clean cup character.
farm_notes: This is a special small lot of Java variety coffee from Finca San Diego Buena Vista in El Socorro town of Acatenango. The Java cultivar originated from Ethiopia, but had stop overs in Java and Cameroon, then finally Central America. The coffee is identifiable by the elongated shape of the seeds/beans, often described as having a "canoe" shape. The Java cultivar is seen throughout parts of Central America, most broadly represented in Nicaragua and Guatemala. It is recognized as producing unique cup flavors, specifically exhibiting tea-like top notes, and mouth cleansing acidity. This lot shows some of those delicate notes in quiet proportion, and I had the most success in pulling them toward the front when keeping the roast to City. San Diego Buena Vista is a 1500 meter farm just outside of Antigua, who we've bought from for more than a decade now, and have gone back for their variety separations of Bourbon, Typica, and Java, year after year. On our visits, we're always impressed with their practices, the way they have separated all the cultivars on the farm, and the beautiful condition of the mill. The mill is a vintage one with amazingly well kept-up machinery and the care is evident at every turn.

name: Guatemala FTO Huehuetenango WP Decaf
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids
appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 15-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination
short_description: Balanced flavors, lightly sweet and malty, capable of deep-toned profiles in dark roasts. Notes of sorghum syrup, malted milk powder, raw almond, baking spice, tea bittering, cocoa. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: This decaf offers balanced flavors, lightly sweet and malty, shifting to deeper toned chocolates in darker roasts. At City+, the fragrance of the ground coffee shows sweet accents of shortbread cookie, cinnamon, and fresh bread dough. The aroma offers glimpses of light brown sugar, bread malt, and a creamy raw cashew note. It's a very pleasant decaf to drink, with convincing sweetness underscored by notes of sorghum syrup and malted milk powder (such as Horlicks), raw almond, baking spices and bittering tea in the aftertaste. The light roasts have a pleasant acidic impression, though body is a bit thin. Full City roasts carry a bit more weight, and also develops pleasant bittering cocoa notes that will punch up through milk.
farm_notes: This decaf comes from a reputable source who like ourselves, selects coffees from their own sourcing efforts based on the cup quality before the coffee is decaffeinated. There's a benefit to having your own coffee decaffeinated, affording you much more insight into how the final product will taste. It's a great plan, and a much more quality-focused effort. This particular lot is sourced from a Fair Trade and NOP Organic cooperative in Huehuetenango, AAPICUC. They currently have around 250 small holders registered with the coop, providing training in sustainable farming specifically to achieve organic certification. This is not only an environmentally focused effort, but also provides a premium payment to farmers as a result. Farmers registered with AAPICUC are also trained to keep bees which has been shown to increase production, even though coffee trees are self-pollinating. The farms span an altitude range of 1300 - 2000 meters. The type of water-process decaffeination method used here leaves the beans a bit mottled and brown, which you can see in the photo. This evens out just fine in the roaster, but you have to pay close attention to color changes as you approach an often subdued first crack.

name: Guatemala Huehuetenango Boqueroncito
short_description: Very versatile coffee, layered sweetness of creamy caramel and unrefined sugars, bright hint of apple, cinnamon-laced cocoa, and dark chocolate with deeper roast development. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: The sweetness in the dry grounds has a whiff of dark sugars, accented by notes of dried raisin and banana chips, along with a sprinkling of bittersweet cocoa powder. Bittersweet roast notes permeate the wet aroma, well-balanced, with accents of baked fruits and cinnamon. In the brewed coffee, the sweetness ranges from unrefined sugars to creamy caramels, offset by roast-toned accents and a moderately bright, fruited dimension. The cup acidity is quite nice at light roast levels, and brings a juicy element to the flavor profile, like pear, and Pink Lady apple. The flavor profile shifts to pleasant bittersweetness that's lightly spiced in the aftertaste, like cinnamon-laced cocoa.
