Full City roasts have very nice roast intensity, chocolate flavors pushing their way to the front, rich dark chocolate, with an accent note of cooked berries. Body is pronounced in all roasts which really adds to the coffee's overall substantial feel. Aurelio del Cerro is a very versatile coffee that brews a sweet cup all along the roast range, and also makes a knockout espresso in the Full City/Full City+ end of the spectrum.
farm_notes: Boqueroncito is a farm very close to another we buy from the Hoja Blanca area of Huehuetenango, Finca Regalito. This area, located in the Northern reaches of Huehue at the border with Chiapas, Mexico is called Cuilco. Both Regalito and Boqueroncito are under the care of the Villatoro family, with Aurelio Villatoro overseeing the wet mill, and Antonio, his nephew, specifically looking after these two farms. We like these coffees and go through several of the process batch samples from the farms to select the best qualities they have to offer. Boqueroncito starts at 1,400 meters above sea level and tops out at just under 1,550 meters. While that's not screaming high altitude for Guatemala, coffee is only planted up to about 1750 meters due to the colder climate here, which slows down the rate of cherry maturation, and aids seed density. The main image for this coffee shows Antonio and his uncle Aurelio, who manage the Boqueroncito farm.

name: Guatemala Libertad Aurelio Del Cerro
short_description: Balanced sweetness and pleasant roast tones are accented by hints of brown sugar, cinnamon, red apple, berry tea, chocolate torte, and more. A very versatile coffee. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: The sweetness in the dry grounds has a whiff of dark sugars and caramel, with accents of dried apple, hazelnuts and bittersweet cocoa. Sweetness and bittering roast notes permeate the wet aroma, well-balanced in middle roasts, with a hint of baked fruit. The sweetness is well-developed at City+, and I wouldn't hesitate to roast lighter too where I think you'll find some brighter cup flavors. Notes of raw sugars offset a bittersweet undercurrent, and the cup profile shows hints of cinnamon, red apple, and blackberry The cup acidity is quite nice at light roast levels, fortified by bright accents of malic fruits and berry tea. Full City roasts have very nice roast intensity, chocolate flavors pushing their way to the front, like flourless torte, and high % cacao bar, along with a subtle berry hint. Body was pronounced in all the roasts we tried, adding to the coffee's overall substantial feel. Aurelio del Cerro is a very versatile coffee in terms of roast level that brews up a sweet cup all along the roast range, and also makes a knockout espresso in the Full City/Full City+ end of the spectrum.
farm_notes: This coffee is from Aurelio Villatoro, a key connection for us in our Huehuetenango coffee buying. Not only does Aurelio have his own farms (Regalito, Boqueroncito, Esperanza, etc...), but he and his family have erected a few wet mill sites in their local communities where they offer a good price for coffee cherry from other small farmers in the region. This lot is from his newest mill in La Libertad region, "Punta del Cerro", that is managed by he and his brother Aler. We like these coffees, and go through several samples of daily process batches from these farms to select the ones that have the best qualities the farm has to offer. The Punta Del Cerro farm is right across the road from the mill, situated in a valley between two steep mountain sides, providing perfect topography for growing coffee, and ideal shade provision from the surrounding natural forest. In this area coffee tops out about 1750 meters due to the colder climate here.

name: Guatemala Xinabajul Aler Villatoro
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Typica Types
short_description: Well-balanced profile of dark sugars and chocolate confections, and should be quite the crowd pleaser. Bittersweet backbone, creamy caramel, marzipan, cinnamon, dried apple. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: The dry fragrance of this lot from Aler Villatoro has a subtle nutty sweetness of caramel and roasted almonds, candied pecan, and cinnamon-laced coffee cake crust. The wet aroma showed more almond tones up front, with deep sugar browning sweetness behind it, toasted marshmallow and milk chocolate. This year's lot has a well-balanced profile of dark sugars and bittersweet confections, and should be quite the crowd pleaser. A bittersweet backbone anchors the cup flavors, contrasted by notes of creamy caramel, marzipan, cinnamon, and a hint of dried apple that lends a pleasant hint of acidity. At Full City, the brew is chocolatey and deep-toned, with notes of dark chocolate torte and truffle that are buoyed by a thick, viscous body. It has all the markers of standout espresso. Even with little rest, my Full City roast yielded a velvety textured shot, cocoa-toned, bean-to-bar dark chocolate, and a raisin-y dried fruit note.
farm_notes: This coffee is from Aler Villatoro, one member of a family group we buy coffee from in the La Libertad district of Huehuetenango. He has two farms in the town of Peña Blanca, both ranging in altitude from 1700 to 1850 meters above sea level. Aler's family have also built out a sizable wet mill operation in the next town over, complete with depulping machine, washing channels, and large cement patios for drying coffee. It's built alongside the river which is the water source for washing the coffee. Aler and his cousin Aurelio also built a mill called "Punta del Cerro" in the neighboring town where they buy and process coffees from other local farmers. (We have some lots from that effort on the way with "del Cerro" in the title). They've played a significant role in our Xinabajul Project that we started more than 15 years ago, connecting us to the coffees of their extended family, as well as the surrounding community of La Libertad. You can read more about the project in our Coffee Library .

name: Guatemala Xinabajul Axel Palacios
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Typica Types
short_description: Delicious confluence of dark sugars and dried fruit hints, with fruited acidity that has a pleasantly grabby aspect. Notes of brown sugar, dried fig and date, orange tea, dark chocolate truffles. City to Full City+. Good for espresso
full_cupping_notes: The ground coffee has notable sweet smells at City roast level, offering notes of caramelized sugars, accented by hints of candied nuts and a lightly spiced sweetness that's a bit like coffee cake. The wet aroma showed more fruit than the grounds, raisins and dried peach, with pungent sweet smells of torched sugar desserts. The brewed coffee has a really nice confluence of dark sugars and dried fruits, like dark brown sugar, dried fig and date. The sweetness is syrupy and delicious in the light roasts, and lingers in the finish. Plump fruit accents in the top end draw out a pleasantly bright acidic impression that gets a bit grabby in the mouthfeel, accentuated by accents of orange tea, and dried apple with the tangy/bittering skin intact. The level of sweetness is excellent at Full City roast level too, with flavor profiles of chocolate confections, truffles, dark chocolate ganache, and a hint of dried berry as it cools.
farm_notes: Like many of his neighbors, Axel Palacios grew up in a coffee family. His great grandfather started planted coffee in Palmira, La Libertad, and packed everything in and out of the mountainous region by mule. Through the years, the land has been divided into separate plots, passed down from one generation to the next. Axel took on his part of the farm in the late 90's, planting in Bourbon, Catuaí and Caturra cultivars. The altitude of his land ranges from 1500 to 1900 meters above sea level. His coffee comes to us through a joint-effort of two local micro-mill owners who are perform farmer outreach on our behalf finding and delivering many, many samples to us of coffees from family members and neighbors alike all over the Huehuetenango region. Each year we make several visits to the area in order to visit as many of these farmers as possible and cup hundreds of samples with the hopes of expanding our " Proyecto Xinabajul " project that we started more than 15 years ago.

name: Hawaii Kona XF Darnall Estate Typica
short_description: * Limit 2 lb per customer. Balanced sweetness opens up to subtle bright tones, and top note hints that are elegant and clean. Molasses, burnt sugar, brown malt, rose hips tea, citrus, cola, pleasantly sweet finish. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: * Limit 2 lb per customer. The fascination with "Kona" coffee is easy to understand. It's grown in the United States, for one. But it also evokes nostalgia for countless vacationers looking to bring a piece of their tropical vacation back home to the mainland. We love Hawaiian coffee too, but let's face it, a lot of what you're served on the island is often stale, roasted poorly, or both. Here's your chance to buy high quality Kona green, and roast it fresh! This lot from Darnall Estate has balanced sweetness that opens up to soft bright tones as it cools, with top note hints that are elegant and clean. The dry fragrance has sweet caramel and unrefined sugar notes, with a touch of baking spices, and herbal tea. Hot water brings on deeper sweet notes with some tartness behind them, like brown sugar with a lemon spritz, along with a scent of Assam black tea when breaking through the crust. The cup flavors are grounded in well-balanced sweetness, with notes of molasses, burnt sugar and brown malt. Top notes hint at tart rose hip tea, citrus, and baking spices, connecting to a pleasantly sweet aftertaste that had a cola aspect. I found this real "sweet spot" in the City to City+ range, which is what this review is based off of. But we've pulled great espresso shots, even with some of our lighter roasts (price is the only reason we haven't tagged this coffee as "good for espresso"). Our notes included molasses sweetness,  hints of date, savory spice, and malic-type acidity that pointed to Asian pear. Mild island coffees like this, moderate in acidity and so well-balanced, are a great choice for un-blended espresso experiments.
farm_notes: The Darnall's excellent Typica is back, and this time we've secured their "XF" quality, which is the highest grade recognized by the Hawaii Department of Agricultural. It refers to both the size of the bean ("screen size"), and the amount of allowable defects in the green. Kona Coffee is grown on the western slopes of the Big Island of Hawaii near the active volcanoes Mauna Loa and Hualalai. That's where you'll find Pam and Ted Darnall's coffee estate, above the small coastal village of Holualoa. The 42 acre Darnall estate is planted in Typica, a variety so common in Kona that it's synonymous with the "Kona" name. While the Typica grown today can be traced back to the late 1800's by way of Guatemala, coffee was first introduced to Kona in the 1820's from Brazil. It wasn't long after this that Pam's great grandfather established agricultural roots in the Kona region farming cattle, pineapple, and eventually coffee. According to Ted and Pam, ever since they started dating, they've dreamed of carrying on the family tradition. They finally fulfilled this dream in 2023 when the current farm site went up for sale. The original owners did not process their own cherries, instead selling to a local wholesaler, which is quite common. The Darnalls have decided to take a more hands-on approach, establishing the "Darnall Estate" name by managing the harvest and processing the coffee themselves, and selling direct. This "XF" lot is 19 screen size, which is similar to Maracaturra, and the larger examples of Pacamara, if you've tried them. Some grinders have a hard time processing large coffee quickly, and just requires a little patience and perhaps some physical encouragement to push toward the burrs. The coffee has a delicate wet process profile, though technically the process style is more like a wet process/honey hybrid. They depulp the cherry and most of the fruit, soak the seeds in tanks for a day, and then move it to the drying patio.

name: Honduras FTO Marcala WP Decaf
cultivar: Caturra Types, Bourbon Types, Typica Types, Modern Hybrids
cultivar_detail: Bourbon, Catuai, Caturra, Lempira, Ihcafe 90, Pacas, and Typica
appearance: 1+ d/300gr, 15-17 Screen - some broken and misshaped beans due to decaffeination
short_description: This Honduras lot flies under the radar as being decaf coffee, especially in light roasts where clean sweetness and sparkling acidity really shine! Notes of raw sugar, tangerine, Meyer lemon, and crisp, light body. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: This Honduras lot flies under the radar as being decaf coffee, especially in light roasts where clean sweetness and sparkling acidity really shine! The dry fragrance shows simple sweet smells, which open up a bit when you add hot water to the grounds. The steam showed elements of molasses and maltose sweetener, along with hints of toasted grains and nuts. The brew shows clean, sweet flavors, accented by notes of raw sugars and crisp fruit, and a pleasant bittersweet aftertaste. It has modest acidity when kept to a lighter roast level, fruited in a way, like peach or apricot. Body is on the light side, and suits the light, crisp flavors. It's sure to please the light roast crowd, but also offers a and an easy decaf to drink more than 1 cup!
farm_notes: This Honduras lot is from the Organic certified COMSA cooperative (Café Organico Marcala, S.A.), located in a southwestern municipality of Marcala, La Paz. The cooperative currently has around 1200 members in areas surrounding Marcala, with farms scattered across an altitude range of 1,300 to 1,700 meters above sea level. It's been a while since we had a Honduras coffee as a decaf, but this was one we couldn't pass up. It has the bright characteristics and balanced flavors that high grown Central American coffees are known for, and the cup clarity struck as as remarkably "un-decaf" in flavor. It was processed with a decaffeination method that utilizes steam to remove nearly 100% of the caffeine from coffee. The plant in Mexico where this coffee was processed has a reputation for producing a decafs that closely resemble the original non-decaf lots, which this coffee can attest to!

name: India Chikmagalur Gemberly Robusta
short_description: Robusta is interesting to taste, but quite different than Arabica. Low sweetness and thick body draw out aggressive roast flavors, with rustic notes of bittering spice, black pepper, kola nut, and tobacco. Full City to French. Good for espresso blending.
full_cupping_notes: It's a Robusta, so don't expect overwhelming (or even underwhelming!) sweetness. But this lot has some cleanliness and definition lacking in many of the Robusta samples we've tasted, and was a surprisingly pleasant coffee to drink! The dry grounds and wet aroma smell pungently spiced, with bitter tea tannins, cocoa, and a dark root-like cola aspect. As brewed coffee, it echoes many of the aforementioned attributes, and offers the incredibly thick body and low acidity Robusta coffee is known for. Dark, pungent roast flavors dominated the cup, accented by complex rustic notes of black pepper, bittering spice, and kola nut. The aftertaste is extremely long and persistent, turning pungent in the finish as would bittering dark roasted coffee, with hints of tannic black tea, and tobacco. Robusta as a blend component ought to be used sparingly, and not take away from the arabicas with which it's blended. Usually I would keep it to around 15% in an espresso blend, but because of the quality of this robusta, I think 25% is a safe start without overpowering the cup.
farm_notes: This Robusta coffee is from Gemberly Estate in the city of Chickmagalur, at the foothills of Mullayanagiri range, probably the most famous coffee region in India. We don't know a whole lot about the farm, other than it ranges in altitude from 1,100 to 1,400 meters above sea leavel.  It was offered to us from a regular supplier who knows we always have an eye open for Robusta that's actually drinkable! I know that doesn't sound like a high bar, but let's face it, the bittering flavor of Robusta is typically far too intense to drink without blending. But this lot has actual sweetness, and offers interesting savory/earthy aromatics that pepper the cup. It's still very intense, and best suited for someone who's tried Robusta before, or is curious what makes Robusta so unique. It's certainly interesting coffee to try on its own, and an opportunity to use an actual high quality Robusta by itself, or play around with using in a blend (start with 25% and adjust from there).

name: Kenya Kiambu Spike AA Lot 2
short_description: Sweetness forward, with well integrated acidity and a sweetly-spiced aroma that lingers in the aftertaste. Notes of maple, blackberry tea, cranberry, goji berry, lemon, tannic tea-like finish. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: We tasted so many nice lots from Spike Farm, and couldn't settle for just one. We were won over by the spiced sweetness, and subtle fruits, and found ourselves buying multiple lots of their AA, AB, and Peaberry out-turns. This second AA selection carries a vibrant structure, with a sweetly-spiced aroma that lingers in the aftertaste. It's not all high notes either, and develops syrupy flavors that will satisfy your sweet tooth. The ground coffee has a scent of brown sugar, accented by hints of dried berry, raisin and clove. The wet aroma is sweetness forward, dark brown sugar, with hints of maple and cinnamon sauce. City and City+ roasts bring out a grounding sweetness of brown sugar, and maple initially, that shift to spiced sarsaparilla as it cools. The brew is tangy and sweet, like dried goji berries, blackberry tea, shifting to a long finish of spiced sugars. The acidic impression comes into focus, underscored by notes of cranberry and lemon, with a hint of orange tea that adds a tannic aspect to the finish. Overall, we found the acidity to be fairly well integrated for Kenya, and doesn't have the super high intensity you might associate with coffee from this region. I think this will be a plus for those who fawn over the fruited sweetness in Kenyan coffee, but not the screaming citric side that often comes with it.
farm_notes: When asking Moses, the farm manager, why they named the farm "Spike", he matter of factly stated that the owner simply liked the name. That's reason enough for me, and certainly a name we'll remember. Spike farm was established about 12 years ago, in Kaira-ini area of Kenya's Kiambu district. This 12 hectare farm sits at 1930 meters above sea level, and is planted in SL 28, and Ruiru 11 varieties, planted in separate blocks. They recently started grafting Ruiru onto SL roots too, also on a separate farm block from the rest. All of the coffee is currently harvested together. However, next year they plan to process coffee from each block and offer variety separations, as well as blends. The coffee is pulped using a small electric pulping machine, then fermented for 72 hours to break down the sticky fruit mucilage stuck to the seed. After, the coffee is washed of the remaining fruit and then dried on raised beds for around 10 days.
watchlist_credential_detail: Sweet Maria's top-rated 2024; multiple AA/AB/Peaberry lots

name: Kenya Nyeri Gaikundo AA
short_description: Raw sugar sweetness and mouth refreshing acidity lie at the heart of Gaikundo's cup profile, with pronounced flavors of raw sugars, high-toned citrus accents, orange, grapefruit, and tart rose hips tea. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: The dry fragrance has a lightly-spiced sweetness to it, with accents of orange, demerara sugar and warming spices. Pouring hot water extracts a cooked sugar smell that's well-balanced, with a hint of fruit pastry. While a more subdued Kenya in some respects, there's still quite a lot to grab on to in the cup. If I had to spotlight Gaikundo's "essence", I'd say it's the interaction of sweetness and mouth-refreshing acidity that's caught our attention. Light roasts show pronounced cup sweetness of semi-refined sugar notes, like demerara and turbinado, with high-toned accents of citrus and tea. That's a winning combination on its own, and the profiles that come from this pairing bring a moderate complexity to the cup. Citrus notes of orange and grapefruit are punchy and bright, accompanied by bittering citrus peel and a pithy orange peel hint. The sweetness has some pungency to it, like torched sugar, with a smoky-sweet note in the aftertaste. Subtle hints of black tea and tart rose hips offer a delicate aspect to the aroma, and add to the palate-cleansing finish.
farm_notes: Gaikundo is a coffee washing station - or "factory" as they're known in Kenya - that is part of the Rumukia Farmer's Cooperative Society. It's near Kagumo town, Nyeri's southern region, with farm altitudes averages around 1600 meters above sea level altitude, but many top 2000. The area is abundant in red volcanic loam soils (common for the area around Mount Kenya), and coffee is usually just one of several other cash crops planted, including tea, corn, and bananas. Gaikundo is part of the Rumukia Farmers Cooperative Society along with 7 other wet mills, including Kiawamururu, Thunguri, and Gatura. As with other good coops in Nyeri, Gaikundo insists farmers separate their coffee cherry by ripeness upon delivery, removing under-ripe and damaged cherry that can have a negative impact in the cup. Small things like this make a huge difference in the resulting coffee. Like most Kenyan wet mills, the coffee at Gaikundo is double washed, meaning that after the outer cherry is removed the fruit-covered seeds are fermented in tanks of water to break down the sticky fruit, then moved to a separate tank of clean water where the remaining fruit is washed away.

name: Kenya Nyeri Igutha AB
short_description: Pour-overs are a real treat, with bright fruits and tangy accents that feel well integrated into the cup sweetness, and an aromatic top end. P iloncillo sugar, orange, green apple, tamarind, Earl Grey, cardamom . City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: Pour-overs are a real treat, with bright fruits and tangy accents that feel well integrated into the cup sweetness, and an aromatic top end.At City roast level, fragrance of the grinds has a red honey note, sweet and syrupy, with spice accents, and hints of dried fruit. The wet aroma has potent Cola-like sweetness, with citrus peel, and a fragrant vanilla note wrapped in. The cup is bright and juicy, with spiced sweetness that fades to tannic black teas and aromatic highlights. Vibrant citrus and sweet tea were the first perceptible flavors, and it wasn't until the coffee cooled a bit that I started to get a clearer picture of what's in store. The sweetness shows hints of minimally processed sugars, like fragrant piloncillo, and dark honey. Tangy flavors of green apple, orange, and tamarind blend nicely with the brisk, bracing acidic impression of long-steeped black tea, along with some whole spice bittering aspects in the finish. The cup aromatics also come alive, with hints of Earl Grey and cardamom adding to that effect. While I preferred City roasts, Igutha produces quite an enjoyable cup at Full City too. Though roast tones are certainly present, I wouldn't call it "bittersweet". It's the milder fruit underlay that kept me coming back for more; dark grape, plum, and red raisin.
farm_notes: This is the AB grade selection from the Igutha wet mill in Nyeri. The wet mill (called a "Factory" in Kenya) operates under the Rugi Farmer's Cooperative Society, an umbrella organization that oversees operations of their associated wet mills, and helps with things like agronomical support to farmers, pre-financing during the harvest season, and marketing the coffees. It's my understanding that Rugi is an older coop, started back in the late 1960's. Igutha currently has around 600 members delivering their coffee cherry to the mill, and farms are typically 1 hectare or less, and at an altitude range of 1700 - 1900 meters. After depulping the coffee, they employ up to 48 hour fermentation time to beak down the sticky fruit mucilage surrounding the seeds. The coffee is then moved to raised drying beds where it will dry for 2-3 weeks. The preferred cultivars are SL-28, and SL-34 bourbon selections, known for good cup quality, especially when growing conditions are favorable. But you also see Batain, Ruiru 11, quite common in Kenya.

name: Kenya Nyeri Kaiguri AA
short_description: Sweetness-driven Kenya that's not all high tones. A middle ground between layered raw sugars and brightly accented hints of citrus and black tea. Makes a great chocolate-laden dark roast too. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: If there's such a thing as a "gateway" Kenya coffee, Kaiguri AA just might be it. What I mean by that is that the flavors bridge the gap between sweetness and acidity and should even appeal to the more acidity-averse coffee drinkers who think Kenya's are all high tones. I've roasted it a few different ways, cupped it, brewed as pour-over and even tried it as espresso, and have found it to be a sweetness-driven coffee more than anything else. The fragrance at City level is tartly sweet, with hints of spice cookie, plum, and dark sugars. The wet aroma has a potent honey sweetness, fragrant caramelized sugars, with hints of cinnamon and raisin. The cup has layered dark sugar sweetness, semi-refined types, like demerara and sucanat, molasses ginger cookie, with some pungent burnt sugar in the finish. Citrus and black tea notes accent the cup, but are not overbearing or out of balance. They bring a nice mouth-cleansing element to the light roasts, without tipping the scales to acidic and sharp. Full City roasts have dark chocolate roast flavors that rival any Central American coffee we have. There's a bittering flourless torte note that gives way to subtle notes of malted grains, and dark berry sauce. It makes a nice espresso too, front-loaded with dark, lightly-sweetened chocolate, and a subtle brine-like aspect brought out hints of salted plum, and chamoy tamarind.
farm_notes: Kaiguri Factory is a part of Mutheka FCS (Farmers Cooperative Society), located in Mukaro, Nyeri, just east of the Aberdare mountains. Mutheka currently has 7 cooperative member "factories", with over 5,000 registered members. Kaiguri factory has coffee cherry catchment and washing station in the area where local farmers (growing altitudes range from 1700 to 1800 meters), who are members of the cooperative, delivery coffee cherry for regional bulking. The coffee is washed, fermented, and laid out on raised beds to dry. The coffee is sorted all along the way, down to the dry milling, and separated by factory out turns. Usually you only see AA (the largest), AB, and Peaberry, but there are other lower grades too, like C and TT. This AA out turn proved to be the best of the bunch that we cupped during the harvest. "AA" signifies screen size, the largest at 17/64" - 19/64" in size. Though not always an indicator of quality, AA's command the highest prices, and so sorting expectations are generally higher as well. The sort of this lot is very nice, some nicks which tends to happen due to the large size of the beans as they pass through the milling equipment, but not much else.

name: Kenya Nyeri Mahiga AB
short_description: Tartly sweet flavors are overlaid with spiced complexity and bright fruits. Notes of currant juice, cranberry sauce, Darjeeling and Orange spice teas, cardamom, fragrant lemongrass, mulled juice. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: At City roast level, the ground coffee had fruits, dark grape and raisin, along with brown sugar, and malty-sweet accents. The wet aroma had the warmth and sweetness of fruit reductions, like red berries cooked with brown sugar, accented with hints of citrus rind and spice. The fruited elements find a nice supporting sweetness in the brew and bring to mind semi-refined sugars like turbinado and sucanat (sugars that still have some molasses content). Fruit flavors are right up front, bringing tart sweetness with it and a bright acidic impression. Notes of cranberry sauce and black currant juice are overlaid with spice notes of cardamom and mace, filling out the flavor profile as it cools. You get these really complex aromatic notes, like Darjeeling and Orange spice teas, and a fragrant lemongrass aspect adds a pleasantly herbaceous dimension. I don't often recommend Full City roasts for Kenya's, but found Full City roasts of Mahiga to be quite juicy and delicious. It still harnesses lots of positive fruit flavors, like mulled grape and plum, along with notable dark chocolate low tones, and thicker body than my City roast. It still produced a moderate level of fruited acidity too, making it a unique dark roasted coffee.
farm_notes: The Mahiga Factory washing station sits at 1800 meters in the Othaya constituency of Nyeri County: With just over 500 farmer members, Mahiga collects and processes the whole coffee cherry for farmer members using a disc depulping machine before fermenting the coffee in order to remove the sticky demucilage layer. After the fruit is easily removed, the seeds are then soaked in clean water where they are completely "washed" of any remaining fruit residue, and then dried on raised beds. Farmers in the region grow mainly SL-28 and SL-34, with small amounts of Ruiru mixed in. Mahiga is one of several coffees we picked up from Othaya Farmer's Cooperative Society (FCS), an FCS that includes an impressive amount of wet mills, 18 in all, and their work in the region dates back to the late 1950s. Coffee is processed and kept separate by day or even weekly deliveries at the factory in order to identify quality. The separated batches are then run through screens in order to separate beans by size, the most common being AA (17/64" to 19/64" screen), AB (15/64" to 17/64" screen), and Peaberry, which are refered to as "outturns". This is the AB outturn. See our video on Kenya post-harvest processing, here.

name: Kenya Nyeri Mutheka AB
short_description: Light roasts satisfied our taste for a brightly-sweet Kenya's, and Full City proved to brew a standout espresso. Juicy texture, apple, pomegranate, Turkish Delight candies and brown sugar. City to Full City. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: This coffee from Mutheka FCS (Kaiguri to be exact) turned out to be a very useful Kenya. Not only does it satisfy our taste for a brightly-sweet coffee, but dark roasts proved to be a standout espresso too. The fragrance of my City roast smelled of caramelized sugar and dark fruit hints, raisins, dried cranberry and ginger chew candy. The wet aroma turned up a caramelized sweetness, with notes of buttery toffee and light caramel, and a spiced-sweet hint of cola. City/City+ roasts have a juicy texture to them, propped up by fruited accents and syrupy sweetness. The cup has a potent brown sugar note, red fruits like apple and pomegranate, tangy golden raisin, and accents of sweet citrus and spices that brings to mind Turkish Delight candies. The acidity is present but not prominent, and offers more of a malic apple aspect in the mouthfeel, fading to tea bittering in the finish. Full City roasts are heavy on the palate and pairs red berry hints with rich dark chocolate. It makes such a creamy shot of espresso (pulled 24 grams of espresso from 18 grams of coffee over 30 seconds). Flavors of syrupy dark chocolate and juicy fruits consolidate in the shot, with notes of plum, black cherry and a vibrant hint of lemon.
farm_notes: This lot is from a station called Kaiguri, which is a part of the Mutheka FCS (Farmers Cooperative Society). Mutheka currently has 7 cooperative member "factories", with over 5,000 registered members. Kaiguri factory has coffee cherry catchment and washing station in the area where local farmers (growing altitudes range from 1700 to 1800 meters), who are members of the cooperative, delivery coffee cherry for regional bulking. The coffee is washed, fermented, and laid out on raised beds to dry. The coffee is sorted all along the way, down to the dry milling, and separated by factory out turns. Usually you only see AA (the largest), AB, and Peaberry, but there are other lower grades too, like C and TT. This AB out turn was one of a few different screen size separations we purchased from Kaiguri. "AB" signifies the size of the bean, which is 15/64" - 17/64" in size. We also have the AA lot available , and a unique opportunity to taste different screen separations from the same supplier. The sort of this lot is very nice, some nicks which tends to happen due to the large size of the beans as they pass through the milling equipment, but not much else.

name: Kenya Nyeri Rukira AA
short_description: Aromatic cup flavors and juicy accents are highlighted in light roasts. The sweetness is marked by complex notes of b erry, pomegranate, tangy citrus, vanilla and a fragrant finish that's tannic and tea-like. City to City+.
full_cupping_notes: This AA lot from Rukira brews an aromatic cup and benefits from lighter roast treatment in order to capture the array of fragrant flavors. Don't get me wrong, it's delicious at Full City too. But you compromise some of those delicate aspects which are what sets it apart. A spiced Darjeeling tea note hangs in the air when grinding a City roast, with hints of dark fruit and heavier sweetness that's like sugar browning in a pan. The wet grounds extract fruited notes of plum and citrus from underlying saccharine sweet smells, caramel, brown sugar and a sprinkling of fragrant baking spices. City roasts are aromatic and sweet, with juicy accents that add vibrant shimmers of fruit to the lighter roasts. The sweetness is marked by dark spices, cardamom and all-spice, along with notes of berry juice, pomegranate, and tangy citrus peel. There's an orange flavor that reminded me of Orange Julius drink, with that sweet citrus flavor up front that finishes with a lingering vanilla note. The cup has a very nice aftertaste, delicate and tea-like, hinting at Chai and Earl Grey, with long tannic bittering on the palate. Makes an excellent pour-over brew!
farm_notes: Rukira is a cooperative wet mill, what is referred to as a "factory" in Kenya terms. Factories are essentially coffee processing sites where coop members sell cherry that will be processed for export. Factories are aligned with farmer members, and operate under a cooperative society: in this case Othaya Farmers Cooperative Society ("FCS"). Rukira is one of several factories under the Othaya umbrella, and is comprised of over 500 members delivering coffee cherry to the mill. The Othaya FCS started in the mid-1950s, ballooning from 250 original members to 15,000 strong today. Altitude of the washing station is just shy of 1900 meters, and you mostly see SL-28 and SL-34, along with a little Ruiru mixed in. Several years back we bought an AB auction lot of Rukira, and we're glad to see it's return. Fruited, bright, sweet, juicy - a real stunner Kenya. This is the AA, larger bean selection (a range of 17/64 to 19/64 of an inch size). Because of the large size, I like to let the roast roll a few seconds beyond what my normal expectation, allowing for proper internal bean development. Overall, I found this coffee to roast easily, color quite uniform as you pass a City roast level. You'll find the occasional "shell", or "hollow bean" post roasting, and we also saw a small amount of peaberries in the sort.

name: Mexico Chiapas La Ramona
cultivar: Bourbon Types, Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids, Typica Types
cultivar_detail: Bourbon, Caturra, Costa Rica 95, Marsellesa, Mundo Novo, Typica
short_description: Ticks off the boxes of a crowd-pleasing brew - balanced sweetness, nutty hints, with modest acidity and dark-toned cocoa. Hints of malt syrup, toffee almond, lemon tea, bittersweet cocoa. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: A balanced Chiapas flavor profile of malty sweetness and nutty hints, with bright accents at light roast levels, and moderate low tones that can be drawn out with deeper development. City+ roasts smelled of almond, mild brown sugar and malt syrup. There's a bittersweet-savory exchange in the aroma, like chocolate pistachio, with a hint of barley tea when breaking through the crust. The cup flavors are right in line with smells, and don't disappoint! Some very nice malt sugar and toffee-nut notes help define the core sweetness in the brew, and fades to more almond and cocoa roast tones in the finish. There's a lemon tea note as it cools that brings out a very pleasant acidic impression too. At Full City, dark-toned cocoa flavors have a sharpness, accented by dark roasted nuts, malted grains, and cocoa bittering aspects in the long finish. This coffee ticks off the boxes of a "crowd-pleasing" brew!
farm_notes: This Chiapas coffee comes from a producer group in Villa Corzo highlands of Chiapas. Farms are very small, typically around 3 to 5 hectares in size. Altitude in this area ranges from around 1300 to 1900 meters above sea level, and farms are planted in a mix of cultivars, such as older Bourbon and Typica types, with other disease resistant hybrids too. Coffee is home processed, meaning each farmer is responsible for processing their harvest down to dried green (with the parchment layer) before delivering to the local mill. Processing small batches in heterogenous way like this can lead to a range of profiles from one farm to the next, and often helps bring complexity to blends. We found this community blend offered structured acidity and mild top notes when roasted light. It's a definite 'crowd pleasing' coffee, and can also be roasted dark for hefty chocolate roast flavors that will work well in espresso.

name: Mexico Tenejapa Valle de Jovel
cultivar: Caturra Types, Modern Hybrids, Typica Types
short_description: Balanced profile with restrained sweetness of unrefined sugars, hefty cocoa roast flavors, accents of loose leaf tea and walnut oil, hints of apple and smoked chocolate. City to Full City+.
full_cupping_notes: The fragrance of the ground coffee has a mild sweetness that hints at brown sugar and corn syrup, with glimpses of milk chocolate, almond and dried fruit. Roast intensity comes through in the wet aroma, burnt sugar and cocoa, along with hints of carrot cake and malt syrup. The cup shows restrained notes of unrefined sugars, accented by loose leaf tea, walnut oil, and surprisingly hefty cocoa roast flavors for a lighter roast. Acidity presents well from City to City+, not super bright, but structured, and a bit like red apple. Full City+ roasts build out body and cocoa character as you might expect. My Full City+ roast developed opaque bittersweetness, with notes of smoked chocolate, roasted nuts and cocoa nibs in the finish. It's a much simpler profile at this roast level, and will stand up well to cream.
farm_notes: This coffee comes from a producer group in San Cristobal de Las Casas, which is also known by its Tzotzil name, Valley de Jovel. The Mayan Tzotzil people are the predominant indigenous goup in Tenejapa, and produce much of the coffee in this region. Farms are very small, typically 2 hectares of coffee or less. Altitude in the Jovel valley reaches 1350 meters above sea level, and farms are planted in a mix of cultivars, such as older Typica types, Caturra, Marsallesa, and Costa Rica 95. Coffee is home processed, meaning each farmer is responsible for processing their harvest down to dried green seeds (with the parchment layer) before delivering it to the local mill where it is prepared for export. Processing small batches in heterogenous way like this can lead to a range of profiles from one farm to the next, and often helps bring complexity to blends. We found this community blend to be overall very well balanced, with structured acidity and mild top notes when roasted light. It's a definite 'crowd pleasing' coffee, and can also be roasted dark for hefty chocolate roast flavors that will work well in espresso too.

name: Nicaragua Buenos Aires Maracaturra
appearance: .2 d/300gr, 18+ Screen; these beans are LARGE, and can be difficult to pass through burr grinders
short_description: City+ splits the difference between subtle aromatics and fully fleshed out sweetness that comes with a bit more roast development. Notes of brown sugar, Assam tea, marzipan, and clove. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: I've really enjoyed brewing my City+ roast, which splits the difference between the subtle aromatic qualities of Maracaturra coffee, and fully fleshed out sweetness that comes with a bit more roast development. The dry fragrance has a smell of toffee, dark sugars, and cinnamon. The wet aroma shows strength in sweetness, dark sugar notes are amplified, brown sugar, a light herbal hint, and barley tea. Our City roast had a light, airy quality, mildly sweet with notes of simple syrup and demerara sugar, with subtle complexity that builds as it cools. It's a lighter profile in terms of body and sweetness, and accents zested citrus, and Assam tea bring out the acidic impression. City+ developed more of a sweetness-driven profile, drawing out flavors of brown sugar and marzipan, along with a hint of clove syrup. Internal roast development can be difficult to achieve with Maracaturras because of the large screen size. For a light City roast, try roasting try pulling as soon as the rolling snaps come to a close. A few latent snaps are fine. Pull too early, and you might taste a little grassiness in the profile from internal underdevelopment. There's a fine line between too light and too dark, but I think this coffee is well worth the risk!
farm_notes: This Maracaturra cultivar selection comes from Cafetalera Finca Buenos Aires based out of the town of Ocotal. The Maracaturra cultivar is a large bean variety of coffee, a cross between Caturra and the so-called "Elephant Bean", Maragogype. It seems to be grown mostly in Nicaragua although I have found nice examples in El Salvador too. Buenos Aires starts 1200 meters above sea level, stretching as high as 1500 meters on the mountain slope. This coffee is wet processed, which means that the whole cherry is mechanically separated from the coffee seed, and then the sticky layer of mucilage is broken down and removed using overnight wet fermentation. This tends to produce higher acidity levels, and often a cleaner, more clear set of cup flavors all around. Maracturra can be tricky to roast due to the enormous bean size requiring a little extra time to develop the inside of the bean. If you have the ability to control heat on your roaster, we've had luck extending the beginning roast leg before 1st crack in order to produce a little more roast consistency from the inside out.

name: Nicaragua Los Alpes
short_description: This Caturra lot from Los Alpes is well-rounded and crowd-pleasing, with the kind of bittersweet profile that's great as black coffee, or paired with cream. Brown sugar, almond, Dutch cocoa, apple. City to Full City+. Good for espresso.
full_cupping_notes: The grinds let off a caramel-y sweet note, accented by almond biscotti cookie, and cocoa. Adding hot water develops dark toffee and caramel notes, with milk chocolate in the steam. Los Alpes brews balanced flavors at a wide range of roasts. The lighter roasts offered subtle, bright accents, whereas bittersweetness and body are developed at Full City and beyond. My City+ brew was well-rounded with a nice interplay of bittersweet tones and a soft hint of acidity. It had a simple brown sugar note to the sweetness, along with accents of toffee-coated almond, Dutch cocoa and apple. My Full City+ roast was a more deep-toned, bodied brew, with high % dark chocolate and a hint of dried coconut in the aftertaste. Both roasts were well-rounded and crowd-pleasing, the kind of simple, bittersweet profiles that can be showcased as black coffee, or paired with cream. It works great as espresso too.
farm_notes: Finca Los Alpes is part of the Buenos Aires family of farms in the Jinotega growing region. We've visited and buy coffees from the other farms, Acopio Suyatal, La Laguna, and of course Buenos Aires, all managed by the Valladarez family who between father Luis Emilio, and son Olman, have been growing coffee in the region for over 50 years. This lot is all Caturra, which is a cultivated mutation of Bourbon that occurred in Brazil in the mid '30s, but was planted in South and Central America mostly in the 1950s. At 1500 meters above sea level, Los Alpes is one of the highest parts of the farm and accessed by a trail leading up the mountain from another coffee plot they manage, Ojo de Agua. It's processed at the Buenos Aires beneficio down below, closer to town, then the wet parchment is moved  to the dry mill in Ocotal. This is one of a dozen lots we purchased from Cafetelera Buenos Aires.

watchlist_credential_detail: 14x CoE winner; 1st place 2023 & 2024; world's largest Maracaturra producer

name: Nicaragua Maracaturra Los Medios
short_description: This medium-sized bean separation of Maracaturra carries the same delicate aromatic aspects of its larger counterpart, with an underlay of caramel sweetness, baking spice, lemongrass and herbal accents. City to Full City.
full_cupping_notes: While this Maracaturra selection is made up of the medium-sized beans, there's no half measures in the cup. It has the same delicate aromatic aspects of our other Maracaturra coffees, with an underlay of caramel sweetness, and moderate acidity for a Nicaraguan coffee when roasted light. The fragrance starts of with a scent of raw sugars and subtle herbal accents in the grinds. Pouring hot water on the coffee develops much deeper caramel notes that are accented by hints of zested citrus and baking spices. City and City+ roast show good clarity in the cup, raw sugars and caramel, interspersed with aromatic hints as the coffee cools. Faint citrus and tea-like flavors combine with hints of ginger powder and roasted barley. There's an herbaceous side that comes off a bit like lemongrass, pleasantly tart, along with a note of fresh basil in the aftertaste. Full City roasts produce heftier chocolate roast flavors, accented by hints of fruit, dried raisin, and an earthy-herbal licorice root hint.
farm_notes: Cafetalera Buenos Aires has offered us a "small" bean Maracaturra selection from their farms. I have quotes around 'small' because it's still on the larger end of the coffee bean size spectrum. (The range is purported to be 16 to 18 screen, measured in 1/64", but I think you will find the occasional smaller/larger exception on both sides of that range). What does this mean in the cup? We found this delicious Maracturra example had hefty sweetness and body, with the bright acidity and delicate top notes of our other Maracaturra's. The Buenos Aires' farms are mostly in Dipilto, and range in altitude from 1200 to 1600 meters above sea level. The Maracaturra cultivar is a large bean variety of coffee, a cross between Caturra and the so-called "Elephant Bean", Maragogype. It seems to be grown mostly in Nicaragua although I have found nice examples in El Salvador too. Buenos Aires is a rather low farm compared to other origins we buy, with this lot coming from about 1200 meters. This coffee is wet processed, which means that the whole cherry is mechanically separated from the coffee seed, and then the sticky layer of mucilage is broken down and removed using overnight wet fermentation. Maracturra can be tricky to roast due to the enormous bean size requiring a little extra time to develop the inside of the bean. Los Medios is a slightly smaller size than standard Maracaturra, but still a factor to consider when roasting. If you have the ability to control heat on your roaster, try a "slow and low" approach, slightly extending the beginning roast leg before 1st crack in order to produce a little more roast consistency from the inside out.
